0.title: How to Behave in the Household of God
0.overview:
First Timothy is a letter from a seasoned apostle to a young pastor — and it is as practical and urgent as anything Paul ever wrote. Timothy had been left in Ephesus to deal with a crisis: false teachers were infecting the church with 'different doctrine,' with myths and endless genealogies, with a distorted use of the law and a spiritualised asceticism that forbade marriage and certain foods. Paul's letter is his pastoral briefing for a young man who has been given a very hard assignment in a very important city.

Ephesus was the capital of the Roman province of Asia — a commercial and religious metropolis, home to the great temple of Artemis, one of the seven wonders of the ancient world. It was a city Paul knew intimately: he had spent nearly three years there on his third missionary journey (Acts 19–20), and the church he planted was one of the most strategic in the Roman East. Now, years later, that church was in danger. The false teachers were not outsiders; they had come from within — perhaps former elders or teachers who had 'made shipwreck of their faith' (1:19–20). Timothy's task was to confront them, silence them, and restore the church to sound doctrine and ordered life.

The letter's great themes weave together seamlessly. There is the primacy of sound doctrine — 'the glorious gospel of the blessed God' (1:11) — against which every false teaching must be measured. There is the ordering of the church: prayer, worship, the qualifications of overseers and deacons, the care of widows, the honour due to elders. There is the call to godliness — a word that appears more often in 1 Timothy than in any other New Testament letter — the practical Christlikeness that is the goal of all authentic teaching. And there are the five 'trustworthy sayings' (1:15; 3:1; 4:9; 2 Tim 2:11; Tit 3:8) — compact theological summaries that sound like early confessions of faith, already familiar in the church before Paul wrote them down.

Above all, this is a letter about the church as 'the household of God, which is the church of the living God, a pillar and buttress of the truth' (3:15). The church is not a voluntary association or a religious club; it is the family of the living God, called to hold up the truth in a world drowning in falsehood. That is what gives urgency to every instruction about doctrine and order and godliness: the stakes are not institutional but cosmic. The household of God must be governed well — because the God who indwells it is the blessed and only Sovereign, King of kings and Lord of lords (6:15).

1.title: The Glorious Gospel and the Worst of Sinners
1.overview:
The first chapter of 1 Timothy moves in a sweeping arc from the failure of false teachers to the triumph of divine mercy in the worst of sinners — and Paul uses himself as exhibit A. The false teachers in Ephesus had turned from the gospel to myths and speculation; Paul responds by giving a compressed but luminous account of what the gospel actually is and what it actually does. It came to him — 'the foremost of sinners,' the man who had blasphemed the name of Christ and hunted down the church — and turned him into an apostle. If the gospel can do that, the false teachers' speculations are not merely wrong; they are tragically impoverished by comparison.

The 'trustworthy saying' of v. 15 — 'Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost' — is one of the great confessions of Christian history. It is not merely autobiography; it is theology. The incarnation (he 'came into the world') was purposive (he came 'to save') and its object was those who least deserved it ('sinners'). Paul places himself at the very bottom of the category, not as false modesty but as the expression of a man who has genuinely seen what he was and what grace did with it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul writes as an apostle 'by command' of God our Saviour and of Christ Jesus our hope — epitage, a royal order, not a volunteering (v.1). To Timothy, his 'true child in the faith': grace, mercy, and peace (v.2).

Both details are chosen for the man reading. Timothy has been left in Ephesus with a job he did not want, facing men who did not want him there, and Paul's first move is to establish that the chain of command runs above them both. And gnesios, 'true', means genuine, legitimately born, the real thing as against a counterfeit — a pointed word in a city full of men who wanted to be teachers and were not (v.7).
verseByVerse.theology:
God Our Saviour, and Mercy Added

Calling the Father 'our Saviour' is unusual in the New Testament and characteristic of the Pastorals (2:3; 4:10; Titus 1:3; 2:10; 3:4). It is not confusion but precision: the Father is Saviour in that salvation was his design and will, the Son in that he accomplished it. In Ephesus the title also had an edge — soter was claimed by emperors and by Artemis, whose temple dominated the city.

Note too the addition to the usual greeting. Paul writes 'grace and peace' to churches; 'grace, mercy, and peace' appears only in the letters to these two men. Grace is favour to the undeserving; mercy is compassion toward the struggling. It is the right word for a tired minister, and it says that God's disposition toward him is not measured by how well he is coping.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Timothy was young (4:12), by temperament not a fighter (2 Tim 1:7), and had been set over a congregation containing older men with strong opinions and ambitions to teach. He needed the apostolic commission standing behind him, and he needed the church to hear Paul call him a true son in a letter read aloud.

Now: 'Christ Jesus our hope' is future-facing, and it is placed at the head of a letter about a difficulty that would not resolve quickly. Anyone in a hard post — in ministry or otherwise — is being told where to look when the situation itself offers nothing to look at.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by command of God our Savior and of Christ Jesus our hope, To Timothy, my true child in the faith: Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by command of God our Saviour.' The word is epitage — a royal order, the term for an edict issued by someone with the authority to compel. Paul does not say he volunteered or was elected. He was commanded.

That matters because of who is reading. Timothy has been left in Ephesus with a job he did not choose, facing men who did not want him there, and he was young and by temperament not a fighter (4:12; 2 Tim 1:7). The first thing Paul establishes is that the chain of command runs above them both.

'God our Saviour' is a striking phrase, because we are used to hearing Saviour of Christ. In the Pastorals it is applied to the Father repeatedly (2:3; 4:10; Titus 1:3; 2:10; 3:4). There is no confusion in it: the Father is Saviour in that salvation was his design and his will, the Son in that he accomplished it. It also had an edge in Ephesus, where soter was a title claimed by emperors and by Artemis, whose temple dominated the city.

'Christ Jesus our hope.' Not our example or our teacher — our hope, and the phrase is future-facing. Paul is writing to a man in a hard post about a difficulty that will not resolve soon, and he names the direction to look.

'To Timothy, my true child in the faith.' Gnesios means genuine, legitimately born, the real thing as against a counterfeit — and the word is chosen with the rest of the letter in view. Ephesus was full of men who wanted to be teachers (v.7) and were not. Timothy is the genuine article, and Paul says so publicly in a letter he knew would be read aloud.

Then a small alteration in the greeting: 'Grace, mercy, and peace.' Paul's letters to churches say grace and peace; mercy appears only in the letters to these two men. Whatever else it signals, it is the right word for a tired minister. Grace is favour to the undeserving; mercy is compassion toward the struggling — and a man carrying a congregation like this one needs to be told that God's disposition toward him is not measured by how well he is coping.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
There is no thanksgiving in this letter. Paul goes straight to the problem: Timothy is to remain at Ephesus — Paul had asked once already — and charge certain persons not to teach any different doctrine (v.3), nor devote themselves to myths and endless genealogies, which promote speculations rather than God's stewardship by faith (v.4).

The aim of the charge is love, from a pure heart, a good conscience and a sincere faith (v.5). Certain persons have swerved from these into empty talk (v.6), wanting to be teachers of the law without understanding either their own words or the matters they pronounce on confidently (v.7).

But the law is good, if used lawfully (v.8) — not laid down for the just but for the lawless and disobedient, the ungodly, the unholy and profane, those who strike their parents, murderers (v.9), the sexually immoral, men who practise homosexuality, enslavers, liars and perjurers, and whatever else is contrary to sound doctrine (v.10) — all measured by the gospel of the glory of the blessed God, with which Paul has been entrusted (v.11).
verseByVerse.theology:
What Teaching Is For

Verse 5 is the key to the letter: the telos — the goal, the point — of the whole charge is love. That is a startling thing to write at the head of six chapters on doctrine, church order and false teachers. Paul is not setting doctrine against love; he is saying what doctrine is for. A theology that never arrives here has failed on its own terms, however correct it is.

The three sources each block a counterfeit. A pure heart — without it, love becomes performance. A good conscience — without it, love becomes compensation, the busy kindness of someone avoiding something. A sincere faith, anypokritos, un-play-acted — without it, love becomes religion, the correct behaviour of a person who does not actually trust God.

The lawful use of the law (v.8) is then the classic Reformed distinction: it restrains evil by threat of penalty, it exposes sin and drives the sinner to Christ (the use pressed in v.9), and it guides those already in Christ. The false teachers had found a fourth use unknown to Scripture — raw material for a speculative system that flattered the interpreter and left every heart where it was.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul diagnoses teaching by its output, not its content — he never troubles to describe the myths. The test is in the words he sets against each other: speculation, open-ended enquiry that never lands, against oikonomia, the ordered running of God's household. 'Endless' is the giveaway. Some subjects are designed never to conclude; that is their attraction, because they can be pursued forever, they make the pursuer feel sophisticated, and they never require him to do anything. Note also the motive named in v.7: first the desire to be a teacher, and the subject found afterwards.

Now: The vice list of vv.9-10 walks down the Ten Commandments, and two of its words need honest handling. Arsenokoitai Paul appears to have coined from the Greek Old Testament of Lev 18:22 and 20:13 — arsenos koiten, a male bed — which is why attempts to narrow it must work against its derivation; the historic reading should be stated plainly rather than softened. But it should be stated where Paul put it: in a list with liars and men who hit their parents, five verses before he calls himself the foremost sinner alive. Any use of verse 10 that leaves the user comfortable has misread the paragraph. And andrapodistais, 'enslavers' — Paul, inside an empire built on slavery, files slave-trading under what is contrary to sound doctrine.

verseByVerse.quote: As I urged you when I was going to Macedonia, remain at Ephesus so that you may charge certain persons not to teach any different doctrine, nor to devote themselves to myths and endless genealogies, which promote speculations rather than the stewardship from God that is by faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No thanksgiving. In almost every letter Paul begins by giving thanks for his readers; here he goes straight to the problem in the third verse. That omission is itself a measure of how serious things were at Ephesus.

'As I urged you when I was going to Macedonia, remain at Ephesus.' Timothy had evidently wanted to leave — the sentence only makes sense that way. Paul had asked him to stay once already and is asking again in writing, which suggests the first request had not settled it. There is nothing shameful in that. A young man had been left holding a difficult church and would rather have been somewhere else, and the New Testament records it without embarrassment.

His job is 'to charge certain persons not to teach any different doctrine.' Note 'certain persons' — Paul knows exactly who they are and does not name them here, though he will name two at the end of the chapter. The verb is heterodidaskalein, another compound Paul seems to have made: to teach other-ly. Not to teach falsehood outright, necessarily, but to teach something of a different kind from what was handed down.

What they were devoted to was 'myths and endless genealogies.' The precise content is debated — probably speculative Jewish elaboration of the Old Testament family lists, possibly early gnostic-style speculation about intermediary beings, quite possibly both. Paul does not bother to describe it, and that is instructive. He diagnoses teaching by its output, not its content.

And here is the diagnosis: such things 'promote speculations rather than the stewardship from God that is by faith.' Two words set against each other. Speculation is open-ended enquiry that never lands; oikonomia is the management of a household — the ordered, practical administration of what God has entrusted to someone.

That is a usable test, and it survives translation into any century. Does this teaching produce endless discussion, or does it get God's household run? The word 'endless' in 'endless genealogies' is the giveaway. Some subjects are designed never to conclude, and their attraction is precisely that: they can be pursued forever, they make the pursuer feel sophisticated, and they never require him to do anything.

verseByVerse.quote: The aim of our charge is love that issues from a pure heart and a good conscience and a sincere faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the key sentence of the paragraph, and one of the most important in the letter. 'The aim of our charge is love.'

The word for aim is telos — the end, the goal, the point of the whole exercise. Everything Timothy has been left in Ephesus to do, all the charging and correcting and teaching, exists to produce love. Not correct opinions, not a settled congregation, not the defeat of the opposition. Love.

That is a startling thing to write at the head of a letter which is about to spend six chapters on doctrine, church order, elders, deacons, widows and false teachers. Paul is not setting doctrine against love. He is telling us what doctrine is for. A theology that does not arrive here has failed on its own terms, however correct it is.

Then three sources are named, and they are not decoration; each blocks a specific counterfeit.

'A pure heart' — the affections uncontaminated, wanting one thing. Without it you get love as a performance, done for an audience or for what it returns. 'A good conscience' — the inner court that has nothing unresolved in it. Paul mentions conscience repeatedly in this letter, and at verse 19 a wrecked conscience is what sinks a man. Without it you get love as compensation, the busy kindness of someone avoiding something. 'A sincere faith' — anypokritos, literally un-play-acted, without a mask. Without it you get love as religion, the correct behaviour of a person who does not actually trust God.

So Paul's test for teaching is not merely 'is it true?' but 'what does it grow?' The false teachers were producing speculation and controversy; the charge was given to produce people who love, out of clean hearts, clear consciences and unfeigned faith. It is worth holding any teaching you are drawn to — and any you are inclined to fight about — against that measure.

verseByVerse.quote: Certain persons, by swerving from these, have wandered away into vain discussion, desiring to be teachers of the law, without understanding either what they are saying or the things about which they make confident assertions.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Certain persons, by swerving from these, have wandered away into vain discussion.' The verb is astocheo — to miss the mark, to shoot wide. The image is an archer, and the target was named in verse 5: love from a pure heart, a good conscience and sincere faith.

Note carefully what that implies. These men are not described as enemies who attacked the target from outside. They aimed at it and missed. They were church people with ambitions to teach, and they went wide — which is a more uncomfortable diagnosis than malice, because it can happen to anyone who stops checking where he is pointing.

'Wandered away into vain discussion' — mataiologia, empty talk. Not false talk necessarily; empty. Talk that has no content and goes nowhere, but generates a great deal of heat and occupies a great deal of time.

Then verse 7 gives the motive, and it is unsparing: 'desiring to be teachers of the law, without understanding either what they are saying or the things about which they make confident assertions.'

The order of that sentence is the whole diagnosis. First comes the desire to be a teacher. The content is secondary — a subject was needed, and the law provided one. Paul is describing men who wanted the standing that comes with teaching and then went looking for something to teach, which is the reverse of how it should work and is not confined to the first century.

And the double ignorance is precisely observed: they do not understand what they are saying, nor the matters they pronounce on. Yet the pronouncing is confident — the verb suggests firm assertion, the tone of a man who has settled the question. That combination, certainty without comprehension, is the reliable signature of this kind of teacher. Genuine understanding usually makes a person more careful, not less.

verseByVerse.quote: Now we know that the law is good, if one uses it lawfully,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul now guards himself against a misunderstanding, and does it in one sentence: 'we know that the law is good, if one uses it lawfully.'

There is a deliberate play in the Greek — nomos used nomimos. The law must be used law-fully. It is a small joke with a serious point.

Notice how careful this is. Paul has just dismissed the would-be teachers of the law, and someone could easily conclude that the problem is the law itself — that the Old Testament is the difficulty and the sooner the church is clear of it the better. That conclusion has been drawn repeatedly in the church's history, and Paul heads it off immediately. The law is good. It is God's, and it is not on trial here.

The problem is a misuse. And the phrase 'if one uses it lawfully' implies there is a proper use and that it can be identified — which is what the next verses supply.

What is the lawful use? Paul answers in the next breath — the law is for the lawless, to arraign them. The Reformed tradition has long distinguished three uses, and they help here. The law restrains evil in society by threat of penalty; it exposes sin and drives the sinner to Christ, which is the use Paul presses in verse 9; and for those already in Christ it remains the guide to a life that pleases God. The false teachers had found a fourth use, unknown to Scripture: raw material for a speculative system that flattered the interpreter and left everybody's heart exactly where it was.

This is worth pausing on for anyone who has watched a doctrine misused. The instinct when something good is being handled badly is to withdraw it, to stop teaching it, to treat the subject as dangerous. Paul does not do that. He does not respond to the abuse of the law by abandoning the law; he responds by explaining what it is for. The remedy for bad use is good use, and it always costs more effort than avoidance.

verseByVerse.quote: understanding this, that the law is not laid down for the just but for the lawless and disobedient, for the ungodly and sinners, for the unholy and profane, for those who strike their fathers and mothers, for murderers, the sexually immoral, men who practice homosexuality, enslavers, liars, perjurers, and whatever else is contrary to sound doctrine,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the proper use, and this is the passage the older text lost behind an ellipsis — quote and commentary together. It deserves its weight.

'The law is not laid down for the just but for the lawless and disobedient.' That sounds odd until you see the point. Paul is not saying a righteous person may ignore God's commands. He is saying the law in its convicting function — as accuser, as the thing that arraigns you — has nothing to say to a man who is already doing what it requires. You do not post a warning notice for people who were never going to do it.

Then the list, and its shape is deliberate. It falls into two halves that track the two tables of the Ten Commandments. First the God-ward failures: lawless, disobedient, ungodly, sinners, unholy, profane. Then the man-ward, and these run in Decalogue order — 'those who strike their fathers and mothers' (the fifth commandment, honour your parents, here at its most violent extreme); 'murderers' (the sixth); 'the sexually immoral' and the next term (the seventh); 'enslavers' (the eighth, do not steal — and note what Paul counts as the worst form of theft); 'liars, perjurers' (the ninth). Paul is walking down the commandments and naming who each one is for.

Two words in that list need honest handling. The first is arsenokoitai, rendered 'men who practise homosexuality'. Paul appears to have coined it, and its parts come straight out of the Greek Old Testament of Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13 — arsenos koiten, a male bed. Attempts to narrow it to exploitation or temple prostitution have to work against that derivation. The historic Christian reading has been the plain one, and it should be stated plainly rather than smuggled or softened.

But it should also be stated in this list, which is where Paul put it, alongside liars and men who hit their parents — and three verses later he will call himself the foremost sinner alive. This is a passage about who the law arraigns, and the answer includes the writer. Any use of verse 10 that leaves the user feeling comfortable has misread the paragraph it sits in.

The second is andrapodistais, 'enslavers' — kidnappers, slave-traders, men who take human beings as property. Paul, writing inside an empire built on slavery, puts slave-trading in a list of things contrary to sound doctrine. That deserves to be said out loud, given how often the New Testament is assumed to have nothing to say on the subject.

And the list ends open: 'and whatever else is contrary to sound doctrine.' The catalogue was never meant to be complete. Sound is a medical word — healthy, whole. Paul's standard for teaching is not merely accuracy but health: doctrine that makes people well. Everything on this list makes people ill.

verseByVerse.quote: in accordance with the gospel of the glory of the blessed God with which I have been entrusted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'In accordance with the gospel of the glory of the blessed God, with which I have been entrusted.'

The phrase is often quoted as 'the glorious gospel', and that is not quite what Paul wrote. It is the gospel of the glory — the gospel that concerns God's glory, that displays it, that has it as its content. The difference is not pedantry. 'Glorious gospel' makes glory an adjective describing the message; 'the gospel of the glory' makes God's glory the thing the message is about.

'The blessed God' is a phrase Paul uses only in this letter (here and 6:15). The word is makarios — the same word that opens each of the Beatitudes. Applied to God it means he is perfectly and self-sufficiently happy: not needing anything, not waiting on circumstances, complete in himself. That is worth holding onto. God did not save anyone out of loneliness or deficiency. He was entirely blessed before he made anything, and the gospel is the overflow of that fullness rather than the remedy for a lack.

And this is the standard against which the whole chapter has been measuring. The myths and genealogies, the confident assertions, the misuse of the law — all of it is judged by whether it accords with this. Paul does not refute the false teachers point by point. He holds them up against the gospel and lets the mismatch do the work.

'With which I have been entrusted.' The verb is passive, and it is the language of a deposit placed in someone's keeping — the same idea he will press on Timothy at 6:20, guard the deposit. Paul did not devise this message and does not own it. He is holding something for its owner, which is the only posture from which anyone can safely correct anybody else's doctrine.

And that word 'entrusted' is what turns the paragraph. Paul has been describing men who wanted to be teachers. Now he remembers that he was made one — and the memory sets off the most personal passage in the letter.

verseByVerse.ref: 1:12–17 – Christ Jesus Came to Save Sinners
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The word 'entrusted' turns the chapter inward. Paul thanks Christ for judging him faithful and appointing him to service (v.12) — though he had been a blasphemer, persecutor and violent man, and received mercy because he acted ignorantly in unbelief (v.13); and the grace of the Lord overflowed for him with faith and love in Christ Jesus (v.14).

Then the trustworthy saying: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom he is the foremost (v.15) — and the reason he received mercy was that Christ might display his perfect patience in him, as a pattern for all who would later believe (v.16). At which the sentence breaks into praise: to the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God, honour and glory forever (v.17).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Present Tense of Verse 15

The four words Paul adds to the saying are the reason it is unforgettable: 'of whom I am the foremost.' Not was — which is what verse 13's catalogue of past crimes leads us to expect, and what most of us would have written. Decades into an apostleship, having planted churches across the empire, Paul's settled estimate of himself is present tense.

That is not theatrical humility. It is what happens to self-knowledge over a long life with God: nearness to light shows more dust, not less. And it has a function here — Paul is about to discipline two men by name, and has spent twelve verses dismantling a group of teachers. He does it from this position. A man who genuinely considers himself the foremost sinner in the room can correct other people without contempt, and nobody else can.

Note also that 'I acted ignorantly in unbelief' is not an excuse — he has just used three brutal words about himself. The Old Testament made provision for sins committed unwittingly and none for sins done with a high hand in deliberate defiance (Num 15:30). Paul is saying he was catastrophically wrong and sincerely so: not innocent, but reachable.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Hybristes, 'insolent opponent', is the ugliest of the three self-descriptions — the violent, arrogant man who enjoys humiliating people — and Paul chose it about himself. Against it stands hyperepleonasen, a double compound meaning super-abounded: where his sin was extreme, grace was more extreme. And note what arrived in the flood — 'faith and love', the very things named as the goal in verse 5. They were not his contribution in response; they came with the grace.

Now: Verse 16 makes Paul's biography a fixed outer limit. Hypotyposis is a sketch or outline drawn so others can see the shape of a thing: if Christ's patience stretched to a man who hunted his people and tried to make them curse his name, no one who comes afterwards can reasonably say their case is too hard. Whatever anyone brings has already been exceeded. And notice where the doxology comes from — not from a doctrine of God in the abstract, but from a man remembering his own conversion and being unable to finish the sentence without worshipping.

verseByVerse.quote: I thank him who has given me strength, Christ Jesus our Lord, because he judged me faithful, appointing me to his service, though formerly I was a blasphemer, persecutor, and insolent opponent. But I received mercy because I had acted ignorantly in unbelief, and the grace of our Lord overflowed for me with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'I thank him who has given me strength, Christ Jesus our Lord, because he judged me faithful, appointing me to his service.'

Stop on 'he judged me faithful'. That is an extraordinary thing for this man to say, and he immediately explains why it is extraordinary: 'though formerly I was a blasphemer, persecutor, and insolent opponent.'

Three words, and they escalate. Blasphemer — he had spoken against the name of Christ, and worse, had tried to make others do it (Acts 26:11). Persecutor — he had hunted people down; Acts records him approving an execution and going house to house dragging off men and women. Insolent opponent is hybristes, from which we get hubris: the violent, arrogant man who enjoys humiliating people. It is the ugliest of the three and Paul chose it about himself.

'But I received mercy because I had acted ignorantly in unbelief.' This needs care, because it can be misread as an excuse, and Paul is not making one — he has just used three brutal words about himself. In the Old Testament there was provision for sins committed unwittingly and none for sins committed with a high hand, in deliberate defiance (Num 15:30). Paul is saying he was on the first side of that line: catastrophically wrong, and sincerely so. Not innocent. Reachable.

Then verse 14, and the verb is enormous: 'the grace of our Lord overflowed for me.' Hyperepleonasen — a double compound, super-abounded, more than filled. Paul is stacking prefixes because ordinary words will not carry it. Where his sin had been extreme, grace was more extreme.

And notice what came with it: grace overflowed 'with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus.' Faith and love were not what Paul contributed in response. They arrived in the flood. The man who had neither was given both — which is the exact answer to the question of verse 5, where love from sincere faith was named as the goal of everything. Here is where such love comes from.

verseByVerse.quote: The saying is trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'The saying is trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance.' This is the first of five such formulas in the Pastorals (3:1; 4:9; 2 Tim 2:11; Titus 3:8), and it appears to flag a line already in circulation — something the churches said, perhaps sang, that Paul is quoting rather than composing.

'That Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners.' Nine words that hold the gospel. Came into the world — he was somewhere else first; this is a pre-existence claim made in passing. To save — purpose, not accident. Sinners — not the promising, not the religious, not the nearly-good.

Then Paul adds four words of his own and they are the reason the verse is unforgettable: 'of whom I am the foremost.'

The tense is the thing. Not was the foremost, which is what we would expect after verse 13's list of past crimes, and what most of us would have written. Am. Present. Decades into an apostleship, having planted churches across the empire and written much of the New Testament, Paul's settled estimate of himself is present tense.

This is not theatrical humility or a man fishing for contradiction. It is what happens to self-knowledge over a long life with God. Nearness to light shows you more dust, not less. The Christian who has walked longest is generally the one least impressed with himself — and the sequence runs the wrong way round from what we assume, because we imagine growth means an improving opinion of ourselves.

And see how it functions here. Paul is about to discipline two men (v.20) and has been dismantling a group of false teachers for twelve verses. He does it from this position. A man who genuinely considers himself the foremost sinner in the room can correct other people without contempt, and nobody else can.

verseByVerse.quote: But I received mercy for this reason, that in me, as the foremost, Jesus Christ might display his perfect patience as an example to those who were to believe in him for eternal life. To the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'But I received mercy for this reason, that in me, as the foremost, Jesus Christ might display his perfect patience as an example to those who were to believe in him for eternal life.'

Paul now explains why he of all people was chosen, and the answer is that he was made an exhibit. The word for example is hypotyposis — a sketch, an outline, a pattern drawn so that others can see the shape of a thing. His conversion was not only for his own sake. It was a demonstration piece.

The logic is generous and worth following. If Christ's patience stretched to a man who hunted his people and tried to make them curse his name, then nobody who comes after can reasonably say their case is too hard. Paul's biography stands as a fixed outer limit: the worst case on record was received. Whatever anyone brings, it has already been exceeded.

'Perfect patience' is makrothymia — long-temperedness, the slowness to boil that endures provocation. And it was on display for years. Christ was patient with Saul of Tarsus for the whole time Saul was doing his worst.

Then Paul cannot hold the sentence any longer and it breaks into praise: 'To the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God, be honour and glory forever and ever. Amen.'

Four titles, and each one answers something. King of the ages — he governs every era, including this troublesome one in Ephesus. Immortal — literally incorruptible, not subject to decay, unlike everything else Timothy is dealing with. Invisible — which is exactly the difficulty of pastoral work: the one you serve cannot be seen, while the opposition is entirely visible. The only God — in a city whose economy ran on the temple of Artemis, that is not a philosophical statement but a stand.

And note where the doxology comes from. It is not attached to a doctrine of God in the abstract; it erupts out of the memory of his own conversion. Paul thinks about what he was and what he received, and cannot get to the end of the sentence without worshipping. That is a fair test of whether the gospel has been understood or merely learned.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul returns to where the chapter began, and the vocabulary of deposit returns with it: the charge is entrusted to Timothy, in accordance with the prophecies once made over him, so that by them he may wage the good warfare (v.18) — holding faith and a good conscience, which some have rejected and so made shipwreck of their faith (v.19); among them Hymenaeus and Alexander, handed over to Satan that they may learn not to blaspheme (v.20).
verseByVerse.theology:
Which Goes First — Conduct or Doctrine

The order in verse 19 is the most practical thing in the chapter. The conscience goes first, and the faith goes down after it. Paul does not describe men who reasoned their way out of Christianity and then began living badly. He describes men who rejected a good conscience — who went on doing what they knew to be wrong — and whose doctrine followed their conduct onto the rocks. Wrong living has to build itself a theology eventually, and it usually manages one.

'Handed over to Satan' is severe language, used elsewhere of putting someone outside the church's fellowship (1 Cor 5:5) — out of the sphere where God's people are and into the world where Satan operates. But the purpose clause changes its colour entirely: 'that they may learn not to blaspheme.' It is remedial, not punitive, the same logic as 2 Thess 3:15 where the disciplined man is warned as a brother rather than treated as an enemy. And 'blaspheme' is the word Paul used of himself in verse 13, before he received mercy. He hands them over hoping for what happened to him.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Something had been prophesied over Timothy at his commissioning (cf. 4:14), and we are not told what. Paul's instruction is that he fight by them — use them as ammunition on the bad days. When ministry goes badly and a man wonders whether he should be doing this at all, one legitimate answer is to remember what was said over him when he began.

Now: The military note — 'wage the good warfare' — is deliberate and recurs (6:12; 2 Tim 2:3-4). Ministry in this letter is not administration but a campaign with an enemy in it. And 'shipwreck' is worth feeling: not a slow drift but a vessel holed and going down, which is what happens when a man keeps sailing while ignoring what his conscience is telling him about the rocks.

verseByVerse.quote: This charge I entrust to you, Timothy, my child, in accordance with the prophecies previously made about you, that by them you may wage the good warfare, holding faith and a good conscience. By rejecting this, some have made shipwreck of their faith, among whom are Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I have handed over to Satan that they may learn not to blaspheme.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'This charge I entrust to you, Timothy, my child.' Paul returns to where the chapter began, and the vocabulary of deposit returns with it — the gospel was entrusted to Paul (v.11), and now the charge is entrusted to Timothy. It is being handed on, and that is how it has always travelled.

'In accordance with the prophecies previously made about you.' Something had been said over Timothy, presumably at his commissioning (4:14 mentions the elders laying hands on him). We are not told what. Paul's point is that Timothy is to fight by them — to use them as ammunition on hard days. When the ministry goes badly and a man wonders whether he should be doing this at all, one legitimate answer is to remember what was said when he began.

'That by them you may wage the good warfare.' The military note is deliberate and will come back (6:12; 2 Tim 2:3-4). Ministry here is not administration; it is a campaign, and there is an enemy.

'Holding faith and a good conscience' — the two things named back in verse 5. And then the warning: 'By rejecting this, some have made shipwreck of their faith.'

Note the order carefully, because it is the most practical thing in the chapter. The conscience goes first, and the faith goes down after it. Paul does not describe men who reasoned their way out of Christianity and then began living badly. He describes men who rejected a good conscience — who kept doing what they knew to be wrong — and whose doctrine followed their conduct onto the rocks. Wrong living has to build itself a theology eventually, and it usually manages one.

Then two names: 'Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I have handed over to Satan that they may learn not to blaspheme.' The phrase is severe and it is used elsewhere of putting someone outside the church's fellowship (1 Cor 5:5) — out of the sphere where God's people are, into the world where Satan operates.

But read the purpose clause, because it changes the colour of the whole thing: 'that they may learn not to blaspheme.' It is remedial, not punitive. Even this is aimed at getting them back — the same logic as 2 Thessalonians 3:15, where the disciplined man is warned as a brother and not treated as an enemy. And note the word 'blaspheme': it is what Paul called himself in verse 13, before he received mercy. He hands them over hoping for what happened to him.

2.title: One Mediator, Many Prayers
2.overview:
Chapter 2 moves from the crisis of false teaching to the ordering of the gathered church — specifically, its prayer life and its conduct in worship. The two sections (prayer for all people, vv. 1–7; men and women in assembly, vv. 8–15) are connected by a single concern: that the church's gathered life should be ordered in a way that reflects the character of the God it worships and that promotes the advance of the gospel in the world.

The theology of vv. 4–6 is among the most profound in the letter: God our Savior 'desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.' The ground of this universal desire is the universal sufficiency of the one Mediator: 'there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all.' This is not universalism — Paul does not say all will be saved, but that God desires it and that the ransom is sufficient for all. The prayer for all people is grounded in this universal saving desire; the preaching to all nations is grounded in the universal sufficiency of the ransom.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul turns from the false teachers to how the church is to conduct itself, and the first item is prayer — supplications, prayers, intercessions and thanksgivings, for all people (v.1), and specifically for kings and those in high positions, so that the church may lead a peaceful and quiet life, godly and dignified (v.2).

This is good and pleasing to God our Saviour (v.3), who desires all people to be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth (v.4). For there is one God and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (v.5), who gave himself as a ransom for all, the testimony given at the proper time (v.6) — and for this Paul was appointed herald, apostle and teacher of the Gentiles, in faith and truth (v.7).
verseByVerse.theology:
'Desires All People to Be Saved'

Verse 4 sits alongside Scripture's equally clear teaching that God chooses and that his purposes do not fail, and serious Christians have answered the tension in more than one way. Some read 'all people' as all kinds of people — which the context supports, since Paul has just named kings and high officials, precisely the class a persecuted church would write off.

The Reformed tradition has more often distinguished two ways Scripture speaks of God's will: his revealed will, what he commands and delights in, and his decretive will, what he has determined actually to bring about. God genuinely takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezek 33:11) and genuinely commands all everywhere to repent; he has also purposed to save a people. The distinction is not an evasion invented for this verse but is required by any reading that takes seriously both the sincerity of the offer and the certainty of the accomplishment.

Verses 5-6 then give the ground, and have the ring of a confession already in circulation. One mediator excludes every other candidate — angels, the speculative intermediaries the false teachers were fascinated by, saints, priests, the church itself. And antilytron is Paul's own compound: a ransom price with 'in place of' on the front. Not merely a payment made for us but a substitute standing where we stood.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Do the arithmetic on verse 2. This letter belongs to the reign of Nero. Paul tells a church in Ephesus to pray — and give thanks — for the emperor who would shortly use Christians as garden torches and eventually have Paul himself executed. There is no suggestion the ruler must deserve it, and no instruction to pray that bad ones be removed. It matches Jeremiah's word to the exiles about Babylon: seek the welfare of the city, and pray to the LORD on its behalf (Jer 29:7).

Now: Notice how modest the aim is — 'a peaceful and quiet life, godly and dignified.' Not influence, not victory, not prosperity. Room to get on with living well. That is a smaller ambition than churches often have for their nations, and Paul thought it enough to pray for. Note also the verb in verse 7: Paul was appointed, set against 1:7 where the troublemakers were 'desiring to be teachers'. One man was placed; the others placed themselves.

verseByVerse.quote: First of all, then, I urge that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings and all who are in high positions, that we may lead a peaceful and quiet life, godly and dignified in every way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'First of all, then, I urge that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people.' Paul has dealt with the false teachers; now he turns to how the church is to conduct itself — and the first item is prayer. Not doctrine, not structure, not strategy against the opposition. Prayer, and prayer for outsiders.

Four words are stacked, and while they overlap they are not identical. Supplications is the word for asking out of need. Prayers is the general term, the God-ward address. Intercessions carries the idea of approaching someone on another's behalf — a petition brought before a superior. And thanksgivings, which is the surprising one in this context, as we shall see.

'For all people' — and that scope governs the paragraph. Not for the church, not for the persecuted, not for the sympathetic. Everyone.

Then verse 2 makes it concrete in the least comfortable way available: 'for kings and all who are in high positions.' Do the arithmetic on that. This letter belongs to the reign of Nero. Paul is telling a church in Ephesus to pray — and to give thanks — for the emperor who would shortly use Christians as garden torches, and who would eventually have Paul himself executed.

There is no suggestion that the ruler must deserve it. Paul does not say pray for good kings, or pray that God would remove bad ones. The instruction is unqualified, and it matches what he wrote to Rome about governing authorities (Rom 13:1) and what Jeremiah told the exiles about Babylon — seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you, and pray to the LORD on its behalf (Jer 29:7). The people of God have generally lived under governments they did not choose and could not respect, and this is the standing instruction.

The purpose given is modest: 'that we may lead a peaceful and quiet life, godly and dignified in every way.' Not that the church may prosper or gain influence or win. Peace and quiet — room to get on with living well. That is a smaller ambition than a modern church often has for its nation, and it is worth noticing that Paul thought it enough to pray for.

verseByVerse.quote: This is good, and it is pleasing in the sight of God our Savior, who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'This is good, and it is pleasing in the sight of God our Saviour, who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.'

The logic connects: pray for everyone, because God's saving concern reaches everyone. The church's prayers are to be as wide as God's desire.

And verse 4 is one of the most discussed sentences in the New Testament, because it sits alongside the Bible's equally clear teaching that God chooses and that his purposes do not fail. If God desires all to be saved, and not all are saved, what follows? Serious Christians have answered in more than one way, and honesty requires setting them out.

Some read 'all people' as all kinds of people — a reading the context supports, since Paul has just named kings and those in high positions, precisely the category a persecuted church might have written off. On this view Paul is saying no class of person is outside the scope of the gospel, which is exactly what he needs to establish to justify verse 1.

The Reformed tradition has more often answered by distinguishing two ways Scripture speaks of God's will. There is his revealed will — what he declares pleases him, what he commands and delights in — and his decretive will, what he has determined actually to bring about. God genuinely takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezek 33:11); he genuinely commands all people everywhere to repent; and he has also purposed to save a people. The distinction is not an evasion invented for this verse. It is required by any reading of the Bible that takes seriously both God's sincere offer and his sovereign accomplishment.

What must not be lost, whichever reading you hold, is the pastoral force Paul intends. He is not writing a lecture on the divine will. He is telling a small, harassed congregation that there is nobody they may treat as beyond praying for — not the magistrate who fined them, not the emperor, not the neighbour who reported them. God's disposition toward the world is not what a frightened church assumes it to be.

verseByVerse.quote: For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all, which is the testimony given at the proper time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all.'

This has the ring of something already in circulation — compact, balanced, easily memorised. Paul is very likely quoting a confession the churches used.

'One God' is the Shema, the first line of Israel's faith, and it lands with force in Ephesus, a city whose economy ran on the temple of Artemis and whose riot in Acts 19 was a two-hour chant of 'Great is Artemis of the Ephesians.'

'One mediator' — a mesites is a go-between, one who stands in the gap and brings two parties together. And the word 'one' is doing heavy work. It excludes every other candidate: not angels, not the speculative intermediary beings the false teachers seem to have been fascinated by, not the saints, not a priest, not the church itself. One. There is a single point of access and it is a person.

Then the astonishing phrase: 'the man Christ Jesus.' Not 'the Son', not 'the Lord' — the man. A mediator must have a genuine footing on both sides, and Paul presses the human side because that is the side in question. Whatever else the incarnation achieved, it produced someone who could stand between.

'Who gave himself as a ransom for all.' The word is antilytron, and Paul has built it: lytron, a ransom price, with anti, in place of, on the front. A substitute-ransom. Jesus did not merely pay for us; he stood where we were standing. And 'gave himself' rules out any picture of a reluctant victim — he was not taken, he handed himself over.

'Which is the testimony given at the proper time.' Kairos — the right moment, not merely a date. History was not marking time until something happened; it was being brought to a particular hour. The same note as Galatians 4:4, the fullness of time.

verseByVerse.quote: For this I was appointed a preacher and an apostle (I am telling the truth, I am not lying), a teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'For this I was appointed a preacher and an apostle... a teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth.' The ransom was for all, and Paul's own commission is the proof that God meant it. He was sent specifically to the outsiders.

Three titles, and they are not synonyms. A preacher is a keryx, a herald — the man who announces a king's decree in the public square, whose job is accurate delivery and who has no licence to edit. An apostle is one sent with authority. A teacher is the one who explains and instructs over time. Announcing, authorisation, patient explanation: the three together describe the whole task.

Then the parenthesis, which is the strange thing in the verse: '(I am telling the truth, I am not lying).' Nobody had accused him in this sentence. Why the protest?

Because of what he has just claimed, and where. That God desires all to be saved, that the ransom was for all, and that Paul is teacher of the Gentiles — these were the fighting words of his ministry. He had been mobbed in Jerusalem for less. Ephesus had Jewish believers in it, and the false teachers wanted to be teachers of the law (1:7). The protest tells us that even here, late in his life, this was still the contested ground.

Note also the verb: Paul was appointed. Set that against 1:7, where the men causing the trouble were 'desiring to be teachers of the law'. One man was placed; the others placed themselves. The whole difference between apostolic ministry and religious ambition is in the voice of that verb, and it explains why Paul can insist on his credentials in one breath and call himself the foremost of sinners in the next. He is not defending a position he took.

And the sphere is named: a teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth. Not in speculation, which is what the rivals dealt in (1:4). The two nouns are the atmosphere his teaching is conducted in — trust toward God, and honesty about what is actually so.

And there is something quietly moving in it. The man who has just called himself the foremost of sinners, and who elsewhere refuses to defend his own reputation, will fight for this. He does not much mind what people think of him. He minds a great deal that they believe the Gentiles are genuinely included.

verseByVerse.ref: 2:8–15 – Men and Women in the Assembly
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul turns to conduct in the gathered church, and addresses each besetting problem in turn. The men are to pray everywhere, lifting holy hands — without anger or quarrelling (v.8). Likewise the women are to adorn themselves respectably, with modesty and self-control, rather than with braided hair, gold, pearls or costly clothes (v.9), but with what befits women professing godliness: good works (v.10).

A woman is to learn quietly and submissively (v.11). Paul does not permit a woman to teach or exercise authority over a man; she is to remain quiet (v.12) — grounding it in Genesis: Adam was formed first, then Eve (v.13), and Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived and became a transgressor (v.14). Yet she will be saved through childbearing, if they continue in faith and love and holiness, with self-control (v.15).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Contested Passage, Read Slowly

The crux of verse 12 is authentein, 'exercise authority', which occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. Some argue it carries a negative shade — to domineer, to usurp — so that Paul forbids only overbearing authority rather than a woman's teaching as such. That is a serious reading held by serious Christians and should not be caricatured.

Two things weigh against it. The wider evidence of the word's use in the period points to plain authority without built-in negative force. And the grammar tells: the two activities joined by 'or' must carry the same value, and didaskein, to teach, is a good thing throughout the Pastorals. If teaching is good, having authority is good too, and Paul is restricting the thing rather than forbidding an abuse of it. This is the reading the ESV follows and the historic Reformed consensus.

The grounds in verses 13-14 are what make the instruction more than local: Paul appeals not to Ephesian culture or to the education available to women — either of which was available to him — but to Genesis. Yet the appeal is about ordering, not worth. The same Genesis says both are made in God's image (Gen 1:27), and the same apostle says that in Christ there is neither male nor female (Gal 3:28). Verse 14 is not a claim that women are more gullible; Paul lays the fall squarely at Adam's door whenever he assigns responsibility (Rom 5:12-19; 1 Cor 15:22).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The specifics of verse 9 identify the actual problem. Elaborately braided hair threaded with gold and pearls was a recognised first-century display requiring slaves and hours to produce, and Roman writers complain of it constantly. The issue is not vanity in the abstract but the importation of social ranking into the assembly — the same problem as the gold-ringed man getting the good seat in James 2:1-4. Note that Paul does not tell wealthy women to look poor; he changes what they are adorned with. Good works is a levelling currency: nobody can outspend anybody on kindness. And note what disqualifies the men's raised hands in verse 8 — not ritual impurity or scandal, but anger and quarrelling. Worship runs on the same track as how you treat people.

Now: Verse 11 is easily misheard. 'Let a woman learn' is a command, and a generous one in a world where formal religious education for women was not assumed. And the scope of verse 12 is narrower than it is often made: Paul is not saying women may not speak — he assumes they pray, and elsewhere that they prophesy (1 Cor 11:5) — nor that they may not teach at all, since Priscilla helped correct Apollos, Timothy's faith came through his mother and grandmother (2 Tim 1:5), and older women are commanded to teach younger ones (Titus 2:3-4). Whatever a church concludes about who teaches, it settles nothing about the value or gifting of the women in it. A restriction on a function is not a verdict on a person, and a congregation where it is felt as one has not read the rest of the letter.

verseByVerse.quote: I desire then that in every place the men should pray, lifting holy hands without anger or quarreling;
verseByVerse.commentary:
'I desire then that in every place the men should pray, lifting holy hands without anger or quarrelling.'

The posture is the ordinary one of the ancient world — standing, hands raised and open, palms up. Jews prayed like this, and so did pagans; it is the natural attitude of someone asking. Paul is not prescribing a technique, and nothing here forbids kneeling or bowing, both of which the Bible also describes. The adjective is where the weight falls: holy hands.

And he immediately says what would make them unholy, and it is not what we might expect. Not ritual impurity. Not scandalous sin. 'Without anger or quarrelling.' The hands are disqualified by the state of the man's relationships.

The word for quarrelling is dialogismos, which can mean disputing or argumentative reasoning — the internal churn of a man rehearsing his case. So the picture is a congregation in which the men stand with hands lifted while carrying grievances against each other, and Paul says the raised hands do not compensate for it.

This is the consistent biblical order and it never changes. Leave your gift at the altar and go and be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer it (Matt 5:23-24). Husbands, live with your wives in an understanding way, so that your prayers may not be hindered (1 Pet 3:7). Worship does not run on a separate track from how you treat people; it runs on the same track, and a blockage in one is a blockage in the other.

Note also 'in every place'. Paul is not describing a local Ephesian arrangement but what he expects of the churches generally, which matters for how the next verses are read.

And there is a plain, unglamorous test here for any Christian man. If your praying feels obstructed, the first place to look is not your technique or your discipline. It is whether there is somebody you are angry with.

verseByVerse.quote: likewise also that women should adorn themselves in respectable apparel, with modesty and self-control, not with braided hair and gold or pearls or costly attire, but with what is proper for women who profess godliness—with good works.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Likewise also that women should adorn themselves in respectable apparel, with modesty and self-control.' The 'likewise' ties this to verse 8: as the men have their besetting problem in the assembly, so the women have theirs. Neither instruction is a general statement about the sex; both address what was actually going wrong in that room.

And the specifics tell us what the problem was: 'not with braided hair and gold or pearls or costly attire.' This is not a rule against tidiness or against jewellery as such. In the first century, elaborately braided hair threaded with gold and pearls was a recognised display — it required slaves and hours to produce, and it existed to announce wealth and rank. Roman writers of the period complain about it constantly. Ephesus was a prosperous city and its church evidently contained women who could afford the display.

So the issue is not vanity in the abstract but the importation of social ranking into the assembly. A poor woman entering a room where wealth was being advertised knew exactly where she stood. It is the same problem James addresses when a man with gold rings gets the good seat (Jas 2:1-4), and the same problem at Corinth where the Lord's Supper had become a display of who had more.

'With modesty and self-control.' The first word means a sense of shame in the good sense — the instinct not to draw improper attention. The second is sophrosyne, soundness of mind, the settled self-mastery that was among the most prized virtues in Greek moral thought. Paul is using vocabulary his readers admired.

Then the positive, which is the point of the whole paragraph: 'but with what is proper for women who profess godliness — with good works.'

He does not tell them to dress down or to look poor. He tells them to change what they are adorned with. The ornament of a Christian woman is her good works, and that is a genuinely levelling standard: a wealthy woman can outspend a poor one on pearls, but nobody can outspend anybody on kindness. Paul has taken the currency of the room and replaced it with one everybody can trade in.

verseByVerse.quote: Let a woman learn quietly with all submissiveness. I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; rather, she is to remain quiet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These two verses are among the most contested in the New Testament, and they should be read slowly, with the actual words in front of us.

Begin with what is easily missed because it sounds restrictive to us: 'Let a woman learn.' That is a command, and in the first century it was a generous one. Formal religious education for women was not assumed in either Jewish or Greek settings. Paul requires it. Whatever else this passage does, it puts women in the class rather than outside the door — and 'with all submissiveness' describes the posture of any learner under teaching, which is how a disciple sits.

Then verse 12: 'I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; rather, she is to remain quiet.'

The crux is authentein, 'exercise authority', which appears nowhere else in the New Testament. Some argue it carries a negative shade — to domineer, to usurp — so that Paul forbids only overbearing authority rather than a woman's teaching as such. That is a serious reading held by serious Christians, and it should not be caricatured.

But two things weigh against it. The wider evidence of the word's use in that period points to plain authority, without built-in negative force. And the grammar of the sentence tells: the two activities joined by 'or' — to teach, and to have authority — must carry the same value, and didaskein, to teach, is a good thing throughout the Pastorals. If teaching is good, then having authority is good too, and Paul is not forbidding an abuse of a thing but restricting the thing itself. This is the reading the ESV follows and the historic Reformed consensus.

Note also the scope, which is narrower than it is often made. Paul is addressing the gathered assembly ('in every place', v.8) and the two functions named: authoritative teaching, and governing authority. He is not saying women may not speak — the same letter assumes they pray and elsewhere he assumes they prophesy (1 Cor 11:5). He is not saying women may not teach at all: Priscilla helped correct Apollos, Timothy's own faith came through his mother and grandmother (2 Tim 1:5), and older women are commanded to teach younger ones (Titus 2:3-4).

It should be said plainly that this is a passage many Christians live inside and find costly, and the honest handling of it is not to pretend the difficulty away in either direction. What Paul gives next is a reason — and where he goes for it is the most important thing in the paragraph.

verseByVerse.quote: For Adam was formed first, then Eve; and Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived and became a transgressor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'For Adam was formed first, then Eve; and Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived and became a transgressor.'

The word to watch is the first one: for. Paul is giving his grounds, and they determine how far the instruction reaches. He does not appeal to Ephesian culture, or to the education available to women, or to the false teaching in that city — all of which would have been available to him and would have limited the application to that situation. He goes to Genesis.

That is why the historic reading has taken the instruction as more than local. Paul reaches behind both Jewish and Greek convention to the creation account itself: 'Adam was formed first, then Eve.' In Scripture, order in creation carries weight — it is the same logic he uses at 1 Corinthians 11, and it is about ordering, not worth. Genesis is emphatic that both are made in the image of God (Gen 1:27), and Paul is emphatic that in Christ there is neither male nor female (Gal 3:28). Whatever verse 13 establishes, it cannot mean women are lesser, because the same apostle denies it.

Verse 14 is harder: 'Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived and became a transgressor.' It should not be read as a claim that women are more gullible — Paul nowhere says that, and elsewhere he lays the fall squarely at Adam's door, twice, in the passages where he is assigning responsibility (Rom 5:12-19; 1 Cor 15:22).

What the verse observes is what happened in the garden: the serpent went around the order God had established, the woman was deceived, and Adam — who was not deceived — went along with it anyway, which is the worse thing. Paul's point is about what occurs when the given order is bypassed, and both parties in Genesis failed in it.

Two guards for holding this. First, Christians who read verse 12 differently generally do so because they weigh authentein and the situation in Ephesus differently, not because they think less of Scripture. Second, and more important pastorally: whatever conclusion a church reaches about who teaches, it settles nothing about the value, gifting or standing of the women in it. A restriction on a function is not a verdict on a person, and any congregation where it is felt as one has failed to read the rest of the letter.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet she will be saved through childbearing—if they continue in faith and love and holiness, with self-control.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Yet she will be saved through childbearing — if they continue in faith and love and holiness, with self-control.'

This is one of the genuinely difficult verses in the New Testament, and the first duty is to say what it cannot mean. It cannot mean that women are saved by having babies. Paul has just said, three chapters into a letter of his own, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners and that there is one mediator between God and men (1:15; 2:5). Whatever verse 15 means, it does not add a second route.

Several readings are held by serious Christians. Some take it as 'saved through the childbearing' — that is, through the birth of Christ, the seed of the woman who crushes the serpent (Gen 3:15). That reads beautifully against verses 13-14, which have just been in the garden, and the Greek has the definite article. Others take 'saved' in the sense of being brought safely through — a promise of God's care in the dangerous business of childbirth, which killed a great many women in that world. Others read it as Paul's answer to false teachers who were forbidding marriage (4:3): a woman's ordinary domestic life is not an obstacle to her salvation but the very sphere in which it works itself out.

The last of these fits the letter's argument best. Paul is dismantling a teaching that despised ordinary life, and against it he insists that a woman is not saved by escaping her circumstances but within them.

Then the grammar does something significant that the ESV preserves: the verse begins with 'she' and ends with 'they'. Whatever the childbearing clause means, the condition attaches to a plural — to Christian women generally, and perhaps to all believers.

And the condition itself is the sentence's real anchor: 'if they continue in faith and love and holiness, with self-control.' Not if they bear children. If they continue in faith. Whatever weight the first half carries, the evidence Paul asks for is exactly what he has asked for from everybody in this letter — faith, love, and the sophrosyne he commended back in verse 9.

It is honest to say that this verse is not fully clear and that good readers differ. What is clear is enough: no woman is saved by anything other than the one mediator, and the life that proves salvation is the same for her as for anyone — continuing in faith, love and holiness.

2.text: <sup>1</sup>First of all, then, I urge that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people,<sup>2</sup>for kings and all who are in high positions, that we may lead a peaceful and quiet life, godly and dignified in every way.<sup>3</sup>This is good, and it is pleasing in the sight of God our Savior,<sup>4</sup>who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.<sup>5</sup>For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus,<sup>6</sup>who gave himself as a ransom for all, which is the testimony given at the proper time.<sup>7</sup>For this I was appointed a preacher and an apostle (I am telling the truth, I am not lying), a teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth.<sup>8</sup>I desire then that in every place the men should pray, lifting holy hands without anger or quarreling;<sup>9</sup>likewise also that women should adorn themselves in respectable apparel, with modesty and self-control, not with braided hair and gold or pearls or costly attire,<sup>10</sup>but with what is proper for women who profess godliness—with good works.<sup>11</sup>Let a woman learn quietly with all submissiveness.<sup>12</sup>I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; rather, she is to remain quiet.<sup>13</sup>For Adam was formed first, then Eve;<sup>14</sup>and Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived and became a transgressor.<sup>15</sup>Yet she will be saved through childbearing—if they continue in faith and love and holiness, with self-control.

3.title: The Household of God
3.overview:
Chapter 3 is the great charter of church office in the Pastoral Epistles. Paul sets out the qualifications for overseers (bishops) and deacons with remarkable concreteness — not primarily a list of theological achievements but a portrait of character, household management, and public reputation. The primary qualification for oversight of the church is being able to manage your own household well: 'for if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God's church?' (v. 5). The church is a household — the household of God — and its leaders must be the kind of people who can run a household well.

The chapter closes (vv. 14–16) with one of the most important ecclesiological statements in the New Testament and one of the most compressed and beautiful Christological confessions: the 'mystery of godliness' — a hymn-like summary of the incarnation, vindication, proclamation, and exaltation of Christ. The church's order and the church's confession belong together: a well-governed household holds up the truth; the truth it holds up is the mystery of godliness, which is Christ himself.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A trustworthy saying: to aspire to the office of overseer is to desire a noble task (v.1). Such a man must be above reproach, a one-woman man, sober-minded, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach (v.2); not a drunkard or violent but gentle, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money (v.3). He must manage his own household well, keeping his children submissive with all dignity (v.4) — for a man who cannot manage his own house will not care for God's church (v.5). He must not be a recent convert, lest he be puffed up and fall into the devil's condemnation (v.6), and he must be well thought of by outsiders, lest he fall into disgrace and the devil's snare (v.7).
verseByVerse.theology:
Character, Not Competence

Count the list. Of some fifteen requirements, exactly one is a skill: 'able to teach'. Everything else concerns what a man is. Any church selecting leaders by gifting, competence or platform has inverted the proportions Paul set — and given what chapter 1 said about men who wanted to teach without understanding what they were saying, the emphasis is deliberate.

'Husband of one wife' — literally a one-woman man — is the most argued phrase here. It cannot require marriage, since Paul was unmarried and commends singleness (1 Cor 7:8); it sits badly as a ban on remarriage after widowhood, since he tells younger widows to remarry (5:14); it may exclude polygamy. Most likely it requires marital faithfulness, which fits the Greek idiom and the tenor of a list concerned with present character rather than an audit of a man's history.

Note also what the four vices of verse 3 have in common. Drink, violence, arguing and money are each a way of handling pressure or appetite badly, and each is invisible to a congregation until far too late. You can assess a man's preaching in twenty minutes; these take years to see. That is precisely why the list is what it is.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: 'Overseer' and 'elder' name the same office in the New Testament — Paul summons the elders of Ephesus and tells them the Spirit made them overseers (Acts 20:17, 28), and Titus moves between the words in consecutive verses (Titus 1:5-7). Hospitality was a serious matter too: inns were dangerous and often brothels, so travelling Christians depended on households opening to them. An overseer's home was to be one of them, which means his family bore the cost of his office.

Now: Two things cut against modern instinct. First, Paul does not treat ambition for office as disqualifying — the desire is good because the thing desired is good. Faced with men grasping at the teacher's role, he does not abolish the office or treat authority as inherently corrupting; he keeps it and raises the bar. Second, verse 7 hands part of the assessment to non-Christians. Neighbours and employers — people who see a man when he is not being religious — get a formal say. Not that they must approve his beliefs; but they must not be able to call him dishonest or cruel. It is a fair question for any Christian: what would your neighbours say if the subject came up?

verseByVerse.quote: The saying is trustworthy: If anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a noble task.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'The saying is trustworthy' — the second of the five such formulas in the Pastorals (1:15; 4:9; 2 Tim 2:11; Titus 3:8). Paul is again quoting something already in circulation.

'If anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a noble task.' Two different verbs, and both are positive. The first means to stretch out toward, to reach for something; the second is plain desire. Paul does not treat wanting this as suspicious.

That is worth registering, because there is a strain of Christian thinking that regards any ambition for office as disqualifying — the only safe candidate being the man who has to be dragged to it. Paul does not say that. He says the desire is good, because the thing desired is good.

The word for the office is episkope, from episkopos — an overseer, one who watches over. In the New Testament this appears to name the same men as 'elder': Paul summons the elders of Ephesus and tells them the Spirit has made them overseers (Acts 20:17, 28), and in Titus he moves between the two words in consecutive verses (Titus 1:5-7). One office, two words — one drawn from age and standing, the other from function.

And what is desired is a 'noble task' — literally a good work. Not a position, not an honour, not a rank. Work. Everything that follows in this chapter is about character rather than ability precisely because the job is not a platform but a labour.

There is also a quiet dignity in calling it an office at all. Ephesus had just been described as full of men who wanted the standing of a teacher (1:7). Paul does not respond by abolishing the position or treating leadership as inherently corrupting. He keeps the office, affirms the desire, and raises the bar — which is the harder and better answer to the abuse of authority than pretending authority should not exist.

Which sets up the whole passage. Paul says the aspiration is legitimate — and then spends fifteen verses on what kind of man may be trusted with it. The desire is welcome; the qualifications are not negotiable.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore an overseer must be above reproach, the husband of one wife, sober-minded, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The list begins with the heading that governs everything after it: an overseer must be 'above reproach'. The word means there is nothing to take hold of — no handle by which he can be seized. Not sinless, which would empty every pulpit. Nothing available to be used against him.

Then 'the husband of one wife', literally a one-woman man, and this is the most argued-over phrase in the list. Four readings have been held. That he must be married, which cannot be right — Paul was not, and commends singleness (1 Cor 7:8). That he must never have remarried after being widowed, which sits badly with Paul's own advice to younger widows to remarry (5:14). That he must not be polygamous, which was possible in that world though uncommon. Or that he must be faithful to his wife — a one-woman man in the plain sense.

The last is most likely, and it fits the Greek idiom and the tenor of the whole list, which is about present character rather than an audit of a man's history. What the phrase requires is a marriage nobody can point at.

Then a run of qualities. 'Sober-minded' and 'self-controlled' — the second is sophron, the soundness of mind Paul commended in 2:9, a man in possession of his own judgement. 'Respectable' is a word for orderly, of good arrangement — a life that is not chaotic.

'Hospitable' is literally a lover of strangers, and in the first century it was a serious matter. Inns were dangerous and often brothels; travelling Christians and itinerant preachers depended on households opening to them. An overseer's home was to be one of them, which means his family bore the cost of his office.

And then the single item on the list that is a skill rather than a character trait: 'able to teach'. One. Out of fifteen requirements, fourteen concern what a man is and one concerns what he can do. Any church selecting leaders by gifting, competence or platform has inverted the proportions Paul set — and given what chapter 1 says about men who wanted to teach without understanding, the emphasis is deliberate.
