verseByVerse.quote: not a drunkard, not violent but gentle, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four more, and they come in two pairs that describe how a man behaves when things are difficult.

'Not a drunkard' — the word is literally one who lingers beside wine. The Bible does not forbid wine and this letter will shortly tell Timothy to take a little for his stomach (5:23). What is in view is the man whose relationship with drink has become the governing fact about his evenings.

'Not violent but gentle.' The first word means a striker — one who hits people. That such a thing needed saying about candidates for church office tells us something about the world Paul was working in. Against it he sets epieikes, that untranslatable word from Philippians 4:5: the man who does not insist on the last inch of what he is owed, who knows when the strict letter would do an injustice.

'Not quarrelsome' — not a fighter, and here it means with words rather than fists. Given chapter 1, this is pointed. Ephesus was full of vain discussion and confident assertion, and it would be easy to conclude that what the church needed was a leader who could out-argue them. Paul says the opposite. A man who enjoys the fight is disqualified from the office, however right he happens to be.

'Not a lover of money.' Money runs through this letter — the false teachers imagining godliness is a means of gain (6:5), the love of money as a root of all kinds of evils (6:10), the rich charged not to be haughty (6:17). A man who loves money will eventually be bought, and everyone will find out what the price was.

Notice what these four have in common. Drink, violence, arguing, money — each is a way of handling pressure or appetite badly, and each is invisible to a congregation until it is far too late. That is why the qualifications are for character rather than performance. You can assess a man's preaching in twenty minutes; these take years to see.

verseByVerse.quote: He must manage his own household well, with all dignity keeping his children submissive, for if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God's church?
verseByVerse.commentary:
'He must manage his own household well, with all dignity keeping his children submissive.' Then the reason, put as a question that answers itself: 'for if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God's church?'

The argument runs from lesser to greater, and it assumes something the modern church often does not: that home and congregation are the same kind of thing. Both are households. The word for 'manage' is the same in both halves of the sentence, and Paul will call the church 'the household of God' eleven verses later (v.15). A man who cannot run the small one cannot be handed the large one.

Note the verb Paul chooses for the church, though, because it changes at the crucial moment. He does not ask how a man will manage God's church. He asks how he will care for it — the same verb used of the Samaritan taking charge of the wounded man at the inn (Luke 10:34-35). Managing a household qualifies a man for something warmer than management.

'With all dignity' probably describes the father's manner rather than the children's — the household is ordered without being harsh. A house kept in line by fear would meet the letter of this requirement and fail its spirit entirely, and Paul has already ruled out the violent man in verse 3.

This requirement has caused a great deal of pain, and it should be handled honestly. It is not a guarantee that a good father's children will all believe; Scripture nowhere promises that, and godly parents have watched children walk away since Genesis. What Paul is describing is the present ordering of a household still under a man's charge — whether his home is a place of evident care and order, or whether it is visibly out of control.

And the principle reaches past elders to everyone. The place where a person's real character is known is the house he lives in. Public competence is easy to manufacture for a few hours a week; nobody sustains a performance in front of the people who see him tired.

verseByVerse.quote: He must not be a recent convert, or he may become puffed up with conceit and fall into the condemnation of the devil. Moreover, he must be well thought of by outsiders, so that he may not fall into disgrace, into a snare of the devil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two final requirements, and each is guarded by a warning about the devil — the only two places in the list where Paul explains what happens if you get it wrong.

'He must not be a recent convert.' The word is neophytos, newly planted — our neophyte. The danger is named exactly: 'or he may become puffed up with conceit and fall into the condemnation of the devil.'

'Puffed up' is an inflation word — swollen with air, larger than the substance warrants. And 'the condemnation of the devil' most likely means the condemnation the devil incurred: the sin that ruined him was pride, and a man promoted before he is ready is being walked along the same road. Give a new believer standing and authority quickly, and you may not be honouring him. You may be endangering him.

This is a hard rule for a church in a hurry, especially a young or growing one that needs leaders now. Paul's answer is that the shortage is not a reason to promote early, because the cost of doing so falls on the man himself.

Then verse 7, and it is the most surprising qualification in the chapter: 'he must be well thought of by outsiders.'

The church does not get to assess its leaders on its own. Paul makes the opinion of non-Christians — neighbours, tradesmen, employers, the people who see the man when he is not being religious — a formal qualification for office. Not that they must approve of his beliefs; the gospel will always offend. But they must not be able to say he is dishonest, or cruel, or unreliable.

The danger is 'disgrace' and 'a snare of the devil' — a trap, the word for a bird-snare. A leader with a bad reputation outside the church is already caught: everything he says about Christ is discounted by the people who know what he is like, and he cannot free himself by arguing. Which is a fair question for any Christian to ask, not only an elder. What would your neighbours say about you if the subject came up?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Deacons likewise must be dignified, not double-tongued, not addicted to much wine, not greedy for dishonest gain (v.8), holding the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience (v.9); and they are to be tested first, then serve if they prove blameless (v.10). The women likewise are to be dignified, not slanderers, sober-minded, faithful in all things (v.11). Deacons are each to be a one-woman man, managing children and household well (v.12) — for those who serve well gain a good standing and great confidence in the faith that is in Christ Jesus (v.13).
verseByVerse.theology:
Wives, or Women Deacons?

Verse 11 is genuinely ambiguous. The Greek gynaikas means either women or wives — the language does not distinguish — and there is no possessive pronoun in the text. The ESV takes it as deacons' wives, since the verse sits inside the deacon paragraph and verse 12 returns to the men.

The other reading, women serving as deacons, has real support: 'likewise' introduces each new group in this chapter (vv.8, 11) as though a third category is named; the qualities match the deacons' own point for point; and no equivalent verse appears about overseers' wives, which would be odd if wives were the subject. Paul also calls Phoebe a diakonos of the church at Cenchreae (Rom 16:1). The passage does not settle it, and honest readers should say so. What is not in doubt is that the same standard of character is required either way.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Notice what is missing from the deacons' list: 'able to teach'. That single skill separated the overseer, and its absence here defines the deacon's work — he serves rather than teaches, while everything else is just as demanding. The office appears to descend from Acts 6, where seven were appointed over the distribution of food. The vices named fit the job exactly: 'double-tongued' is a precise hazard for men moving between households hearing everybody's business, and 'greedy for dishonest gain' matters when relief funds pass through your hands with no ledger anybody checks. 'Not slanderers' in verse 11 uses diabolos, the devil's own title, which should sober anyone who has enjoyed passing something on.

Now: Verse 10's order is the one most churches reverse. Test first, then appoint — and the testing is by time, not examination (dokimazo, the assayer's word). Appointing a man and finding out afterwards is how most congregations actually proceed and how most of them come to grief. And verse 13 attaches a striking promise to practical service: not promotion but parrhesia, the boldness to speak freely. A man who has carried food to widows for years ends up with a settledness in the faith that study alone does not produce. Serving well does something to the server.

verseByVerse.quote: Deacons likewise must be dignified, not double-tongued, not addicted to much wine, not greedy for dishonest gain. They must hold the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience. And let them also be tested first; then let them serve as deacons if they prove themselves blameless.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Deacons likewise.' The word ties the second office to the first — same seriousness, different function. Diakonos means servant, and the office appears to descend from Acts 6, where seven men were appointed to handle the distribution of food so that the apostles could give themselves to prayer and the word.

Notice at once what is missing from this list. There is no 'able to teach'. That single skill separated the overseer, and its absence here defines the deacon's work: he serves rather than teaches. Everything else — the character, the testing, the blamelessness — is just as demanding.

Four negatives. 'Dignified' first, the same word used of the overseer's household manner. 'Not double-tongued' — literally two-worded, saying one thing here and another there. It is a precise hazard for men who move between households collecting and distributing, hearing everybody's business. A deacon who repeats in one house what he heard in another destroys the trust the job runs on.

'Not addicted to much wine' and 'not greedy for dishonest gain' — and the second is exact for the office. Deacons handled money for the poor. The phrase means eager for shameful profit, and the temptation is obvious: funds passing through your hands with no ledger anybody checks.

Then verse 9, which is the positive at the centre: 'They must hold the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience.' Deacons are not required to expound the faith, but they must hold it — and hold it with a conscience that is clean. That phrase has already appeared twice (1:5, 19), and it is the letter's steady concern. A man may distribute bread faultlessly while carrying something unresolved, and Paul will not have it.

And verse 10 gives the procedure: 'let them also be tested first; then let them serve.' Not tested by an examination but by time — the verb is the assayer's word again, dokimazo, proving metal. Paul's order is: observe the man, then appoint him. The reverse order — appoint him and find out afterwards — is how most churches actually do it, and it is how most of them come to grief.

verseByVerse.quote: Their wives likewise must be dignified, not slanderers, but sober-minded, faithful in all things. Let deacons each be the husband of one wife, managing their children and their own households well. For those who serve well as deacons gain a good standing for themselves and also great confidence in the faith that is in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Their wives likewise must be dignified, not slanderers, but sober-minded, faithful in all things.'

The Greek word is simply gynaikas, which means either women or wives — the language does not distinguish, and there is no possessive pronoun in the text. So the verse is genuinely ambiguous, and the choice matters.

Two readings are held by serious Christians. The ESV takes it as deacons' wives, on the ground that the verse sits inside the deacon paragraph and verse 12 returns to the men. The other takes it as women who serve as deacons, and has real support: the word 'likewise' introduces each new group in this chapter (v.8, v.11) as though a third category is being named; the qualities listed match the deacons' own point for point; and no equivalent verse appears about overseers' wives, which would be strange if wives were the subject. Paul also calls Phoebe a diakonos of the church at Cenchreae (Rom 16:1).

The passage does not settle it, and honest readers should say so. What is not in doubt is that the same standard of character is required either way, and that the qualities are the ones this letter keeps returning to.

'Not slanderers' is the counterpart to the deacons' 'not double-tongued' — the word is diabolos, the same word used of the devil, whose name means accuser. Careless talk about people is given the devil's own title, which should sober anyone who has ever enjoyed passing something on.

Then verse 13, and it is a promise rather than a requirement: 'those who serve well as deacons gain a good standing for themselves and also great confidence in the faith.' Parrhesia — the boldness of a man who can speak freely, the word used of the apostles before the council.

That is a striking thing to attach to practical service. Paul does not promise deacons promotion; he promises them assurance. A man who has carried food to widows for years, quietly and honestly, ends up with a settledness in the faith that no amount of study produces on its own. Serving well does something to the server.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul states the letter's purpose: he hopes to come soon, but writes in case he is delayed (v.14), so that they may know how to behave in the household of God — the church of the living God, a pillar and buttress of the truth (v.15).

And then the chapter of overseers, deacons, wine and money opens into a hymn: great indeed is the mystery of godliness — he was manifested in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among the nations, believed on in the world, taken up in glory (v.16).
verseByVerse.theology:
Pillar and Buttress — and Which Way Round

Everyone in Ephesus knew what a pillar was. The temple of Artemis had well over a hundred of them, sixty feet high, one of the seven wonders of the world. Paul takes the architectural vocabulary of the most famous building in Asia and applies it to congregations meeting in houses — and calls their God the living God, an adjective with teeth in a city whose great temple housed an image that could not move.

But get the relation the right way round, because it is often inverted. The church does not create the truth or authenticate it. A pillar does not make the roof; it holds it up where people can see it. The truth stands on its own, and the church's task is to hold it visibly in place — precisely what the false teachers of chapter 1 were failing to do. That gives a congregation its shape: not primarily a service provider, a campaign or a community centre, but the structure by which the truth about God is held up in a town.

The hymn of verse 16 has six lines, each beginning with a verb, and every verb is passive. Christ is the subject throughout and the actor nowhere: God does all of it. 'Manifested in the flesh' means he existed before he appeared, and in real flesh — the line rules out both early errors at once. 'Vindicated by the Spirit' is the language of justification: condemned by a Roman court, he was declared to be in the right by a higher one.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The letter exists because of a contingency — Paul intends to come and may not. A good deal of Scripture came to us that way; he could not get to Thessalonica either, and we have two letters because of it. And 'household of God' is what chapter 3 has been building toward: the overseer must manage his own household because the church is one. A household in that world was not a nuclear family but an extended body — kin, servants, dependants — with an order to it and a head.

Now: Note the least likely pair in the hymn: 'proclaimed among the nations, believed on in the world.' The other lines are about Christ himself; these two are about what happened next, and they are the improbable part. A crucified provincial was announced to an empire, and people believed it — and Paul is writing to a church in Ephesus that exists because that line came true. Notice too where the hymn sits: straight after a chapter on wine, money, household management and reputation. The rules are not religious housekeeping. They exist so that the pillar stands straight and this can be seen from the street.

verseByVerse.quote: I hope to come to you soon, but I am writing these things to you so that, if I delay, you may know how one ought to behave in the household of God, which is the church of the living God, a pillar and buttress of the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'I hope to come to you soon, but I am writing these things to you so that, if I delay, you may know how one ought to behave in the household of God.'

Here is the letter's own statement of purpose, and it is worth noting the honesty of it. Paul intends to come. He may not. The letter exists because of a contingency, which is how a great deal of Scripture came to be written — Paul could not get to Thessalonica either, and we have two letters because of it.

'The household of God.' Everything in chapter 3 has been building here. The overseer must manage his own household because the church is one; the deacons serve in it; and now the whole is named. A household in that world was not a nuclear family but an extended body — kin, servants, dependants — with an order to it and a head. The church is that, and it is God's.

Then two further descriptions, and they lift the sentence enormously. 'The church of the living God' — and the adjective has teeth in Ephesus, whose great temple housed an image that could not move. And 'a pillar and buttress of the truth'.

Anyone in that city knew what a pillar was. The temple of Artemis had well over a hundred of them, sixty feet high, one of the seven wonders of the world. A pillar holds something up so it can be seen; a buttress is the foundation-support that keeps it from shifting. Paul takes the architectural vocabulary of the most famous building in Asia and applies it to a congregation meeting in houses.

Get the relation the right way round, though, because it is often inverted. The church does not create the truth or authenticate it. A pillar does not make the roof; it holds it up where people can see it. The truth stands on its own and the church's task is to hold it visibly in place — which is exactly what the false teachers of chapter 1 were failing to do.

And that gives the church's job a shape. A congregation is not primarily a service provider, a campaign, or a community centre. It is the structure by which the truth about God is held up in a town so that people can see it.

verseByVerse.quote: Great indeed, we confess, is the mystery of godliness: He was manifested in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among the nations, believed on in the world, taken up in glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Great indeed, we confess, is the mystery of godliness' — and then the sentence changes shape entirely. What follows is rhythmic, balanced, and almost certainly a hymn the churches sang. Paul quotes it whole.

Six lines, each beginning with a verb, and every one of them passive: he was manifested, vindicated, seen, proclaimed, believed on, taken up. Christ is the subject throughout and the actor nowhere. God is doing all of it.

'Manifested in the flesh' — he was manifested, which means he existed before he appeared. And in flesh: not a semblance, not a costume, but the real thing. The first line rules out the two errors the early church had to fight, that he was not truly divine and that he was not truly human.

'Vindicated by the Spirit' — the word is justified, declared to be in the right. He had been condemned by a Roman court and executed as a criminal; the resurrection by the Spirit was the higher court overturning the verdict.

'Seen by angels' — the unseen world watched. Angels appear at every hinge of his life: the announcement, the birth, the wilderness, Gethsemane, the empty tomb, the ascension. Peter says they long to look into these things (1 Pet 1:12).

'Proclaimed among the nations, believed on in the world' — and this is the astonishing pair, because it is the least likely thing on the list. The other lines are about him; these two are about what happened next. A crucified provincial was announced to the empire, and people believed it. Paul is writing to a church in Ephesus that exists because that line came true.

'Taken up in glory' — the ascension, and the hymn ends where he now is.

Notice where this sits. Paul has spent a chapter on overseers, deacons, wine, money, household management and reputation — the unglamorous machinery of a working church. Then he says: and this is what it is all for. The rules about drink and quarrelling are not religious housekeeping. They exist so that the pillar stands straight and this can be seen from the street.

3.text: <sup>1</sup>The saying is trustworthy: If anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a noble task.<sup>2</sup>Therefore an overseer must be above reproach, the husband of one wife, sober-minded, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach,<sup>3</sup>not a drunkard, not violent but gentle, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money.<sup>4</sup>He must manage his own household well, with all dignity keeping his children submissive,<sup>5</sup>for if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God's church?<sup>6</sup>He must not be a recent convert, or he may become puffed up with conceit and fall into the condemnation of the devil.<sup>7</sup>Moreover, he must be well thought of by outsiders, so that he may not fall into disgrace, into a snare of the devil.<sup>8</sup>Deacons likewise must be dignified, not double-tongued, not addicted to much wine, not greedy for dishonest gain.<sup>9</sup>They must hold the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience.<sup>10</sup>And let them also be tested first; then let them serve as deacons if they prove themselves blameless.<sup>11</sup>Their wives likewise must be dignified, not slanderers, but sober-minded, faithful in all things.<sup>12</sup>Let deacons each be the husband of one wife, managing their children and their own households well.<sup>13</sup>For those who serve well as deacons gain a good standing for themselves and also great confidence in the faith that is in Christ Jesus.<sup>14</sup>I hope to come to you soon, but I am writing these things to you so that,<sup>15</sup>if I delay, you may know how one ought to behave in the household of God, which is the church of the living God, a pillar and buttress of the truth.<sup>16</sup>Great indeed, we confess, is the mystery of godliness: He was manifested in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among the nations, believed on in the world, taken up in glory.

4.title: A Good Servant of Christ Jesus
4.overview:
Chapter 4 brings the letter into sharp personal focus on Timothy himself. After addressing the congregation's prayer life and the church's officers, Paul now turns to the young pastor: here is what you must do, here is how you must live, here is what you must not neglect. The chapter is one of the richest pastoral training texts in the New Testament — a manual for the minister who wants to be 'a good servant of Christ Jesus.'

The chapter is framed by a warning (vv. 1–5) and a training programme (vv. 6–16). The warning is eschatological: the Spirit explicitly says that in later times some will depart from the faith. The signs are already visible in Ephesus — teachers who forbid marriage and require abstinence from foods that God created. The response is twofold: correct the false teaching with truth, and train yourself in godliness. Both activities — teaching and training — are the irreducible core of pastoral work.

verseByVerse.ref: 4:1–5 – Some Will Depart from the Faith
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Spirit's explicit prediction of apostasy is sobering: departing from the faith is not a theoretical possibility but a prophesied reality. The mechanism is 'devoting themselves to deceitful spirits and teachings of demons' — a description that locates the false teaching's ultimate origin in the spiritual realm, whatever its immediate human vehicles. The specific content of the false teaching — forbidding marriage and requiring abstinence from foods — is a form of asceticism that denies the goodness of creation. Paul's counter-argument is a theology of creation: everything God created is good (Gen 1:31), and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving.

The phrase 'it is made holy by the word of God and prayer' (v. 5) is one of the clearest statements of the theology of blessing in the New Testament. The word of God — the affirmation that creation is good — and prayer — the act of receiving food in thankfulness — together consecrate the ordinary act of eating as a holy activity. The false teachers had introduced a false sacred/secular divide; Paul demolishes it with creation theology.
verseByVerse.theology: The false teaching addressed here is a proto-Gnostic dualism that views the material world as spiritually inferior or corrupt. Paul's response draws on the thick biblical theology of creation: 'everything created by God is good' (v. 4, echoing Genesis 1). This is the foundation of a robust Christian approach to embodied life — food, marriage, work, rest, beauty — all of it is the gift of the good Creator and is to be received with gratitude, not escaped with asceticism. The Reformation recovered this creation theology against a medieval piety that often devalued marriage and bodily life in favour of celibate religious orders. Luther's marriage to Katharina von Bora was a theological statement as much as a personal one.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Ephesian false teachers' forbidding of marriage and certain foods was probably connected to a proto-Gnostic view that matter is evil and salvation means escaping it. Marriage — which involves bodies, sexuality, and the propagation of more bodily life — was suspect. Food restrictions marked out a spiritual elite.

Now: Every generation has its version of the false sacred/secular divide — the notion that 'spiritual' Christians eat only certain diets, abstain from certain pleasures, or avoid certain vocations. Paul's creation theology is the corrective: receive everything God has made with thanksgiving, and it is holy. The problem is never God's good creation; the problem is the fallen heart that either worships the creation or despises it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the Spirit expressly says that in later times some will depart from the faith by devoting themselves to deceitful spirits and teachings of demons, through the insincerity of liars whose consciences are seared, who forbid marriage and require abstinence from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving by those who believe and know the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary: The Spirit's explicit prediction — not a vague warning but a specific prophecy — shows that Paul is not surprised by the Ephesian crisis. The departure from the faith has a specific mechanism: 'deceitful spirits and teachings of demons.' False doctrine has a dark paternity; it is not merely human error but Satanic interference. The teachers themselves are described as having 'seared' consciences — the word evokes a cauterised wound, a surface that can no longer feel. The repeated suppression of conscience produces this: a person who can teach falsehood without internal friction, who has lost the capacity to feel the wrongness of what they say. This is the end point of the process Paul warned about in 1:19.

verseByVerse.quote: For everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving, for it is made holy by the word of God and prayer.
verseByVerse.commentary: The theological counter to asceticism is creation theology. 'Everything created by God is good' — a direct echo of Genesis 1:31 ('God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good'). The fall has not unmade the goodness of creation; sin has distorted humanity's relationship to creation (we now lust after it, fear it, or despise it, instead of receiving it in gratitude), but the creation itself retains its God-given goodness. 'Made holy by the word of God and prayer' describes the act of grace that surrounds a meal: God has said it is good (the word), and we receive it with thanks (prayer). In that frame, eating a meal becomes a liturgical act — a small act of worship in which the Creator is honoured through the creature's gratitude.

verseByVerse.ref: 4:6–16 – A Good Servant of Christ Jesus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
This section is Paul's personal training programme for Timothy — and through Timothy, for every gospel minister. It moves through several related imperatives: be nourished on sound doctrine (v. 6); avoid irreverent myths (v. 7); train yourself for godliness (vv. 7–8); labour and strive because you have hoped in the living God (vv. 9–10); command and teach (v. 11); don't let anyone despise your youth but be an example (vv. 12); devote yourself to the public ministry of the word (v. 13); don't neglect your gift (v. 14); practise these things (v. 15); keep a close watch on yourself and the teaching (v. 16).

The centrepiece is the comparison between physical training and training in godliness (vv. 7–8). Physical training has value — Paul is not dismissive of the body — but it profits only 'for a little while.' Godliness, by contrast, 'holds promise for the present life and also for the life to come.' The minister who devotes himself to the spiritual disciplines of word, prayer, and example is investing in something eternal; the minister who neglects them in favour of more visible activities is spending the capital of his ministry without replenishing it.
verseByVerse.theology: The fourth trustworthy saying — 'we have put our hope in the living God, who is the Savior of all people, especially of those who believe' (v. 10) — is theologically rich. 'Savior of all people' does not teach universalism; it teaches the universal providence of God that preserves all human life and gives common grace to all (cf. Matt 5:45; Acts 14:17; 17:25). 'Especially of those who believe' distinguishes the saving grace of the gospel from the preserving grace of common providence. All people benefit from God's providential care; believers benefit from his saving grace. This distinction between general and special grace is one of the building blocks of Reformed theology's account of God's relationship to the world.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Timothy was young and may have felt intimidated by older, more experienced members of the congregation — especially those who questioned his authority. Paul's instruction is to outrun his critics not by asserting his authority but by being an example: 'in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity.' The best answer to those who despise youth is a life that commands respect.

Now: The 'training for godliness' model — practice, discipline, repetition, formation — is countercultural in an age of instant results and performance metrics. Ministry is not a set of deliverables; it is the formation of a person over years of faithful practice. The minister who wants to be useful at fifty must begin the disciplines of word, prayer, and example at twenty-five.

verseByVerse.quote: If you put these things before the brothers, you will be a good servant of Christ Jesus, being trained in the words of the faith and of the good doctrine that you have followed. Have nothing to do with irreverent, silly myths. Rather train yourself for godliness; for while bodily training is of some value, godliness is of value in every way, as it holds promise for the present life and also for the life to come.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'A good servant of Christ Jesus' — the word for 'servant' is the same word behind 'deacon.' The minister of the gospel is first a servant, not an authority. Being 'trained in the words of the faith and of the good doctrine' — suggesting continuous nourishment, an ongoing diet. The minister who is not being fed by the word cannot feed others with it. 'Train yourself for godliness' — the word is the root of 'gymnasium.' The image is of disciplined, repetitive, patient exercise. Godliness does not arrive by inspiration alone; it is formed by practice — the regular disciplines of prayer, word, worship, obedience — sustained over years until they become the natural shape of the person.

verseByVerse.quote: The saying is trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance. For to this end we toil and strive, because we have our hope set on the living God, who is the Savior of all people, especially of those who believe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The trustworthy saying here (the third in the Pastorals) points to the truth just articulated: godliness holds promise for the present life and the life to come. And Paul grounds the labour and striving in hope: we toil because we have hoped in the living God. The ministry is not driven by duty or compulsion but by hope — the confident expectation that the God who saves, the God who raised Jesus, the God who promises life to come, will not let faithful work be in vain. 'We toil and strive' — kopiaō and agōnizomai — are strenuous words, implying exhausting labour and athletic contest. The ministry of the gospel is not comfortable work; it requires everything. But the living God sustains those who have set their hope on him.

"The Savior of all people, especially of those who believe" — does this mean everyone is saved in the end? No; Paul is emphatic everywhere that salvation is through faith. Two sound readings: God is the preserver of all — his common goodness sustains every life that draws breath (so Calvin) — and savingly the Savior of those who believe; or, he is the only Savior there is, offered to all, effective for believers. Either way, "especially" marks the line between God's kindness to all and his salvation of his own. The verse widens the offer; it does not remove the need for faith.

verseByVerse.quote: Command and teach these things. Let no one despise you for your youth, but set the believers an example in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity. Until I come, devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation, to teaching. Do not neglect the gift you have, which was given you by prophecy when the council of elders laid their hands on you.
verseByVerse.commentary: The fivefold example Timothy must set — speech, conduct, love, faith, purity — covers the whole person: words, actions, affections, convictions, sexual integrity. These are not a checklist but a portrait of a person who has been genuinely transformed by the gospel they proclaim. 'The public reading of Scripture, exhortation, teaching' — three elements of the Sunday gathering, in order: first the word is read (heard), then exhorted (applied to the conscience), then taught (explained and argued). The ministry of the word is the heart of the gathered church's life. The gift given at Timothy's ordination — whatever specific capacity it conferred — is not to be neglected through fear or distraction. It is to be fanned into flame (2 Tim 1:6).

verseByVerse.quote: Practice these things, immerse yourself in them, so that all may see your progress. Keep a close watch on yourself and on the teaching. Persist in this, for by so doing you will save both yourself and your hearers.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Immerse yourself in them' — literally 'be in them,' a phrase suggesting total absorption, the way a person is 'in' the water when they are swimming. Progress in ministry and in godliness is observable: people see it. They see the minister becoming more Christ-like, more patient, more insightful, more loving — and that visible progress is itself a form of ministry. 'Keep a close watch on yourself and on the teaching' — both. Self-watch without doctrinal watch produces a morally respectable person who teaches error; doctrinal watch without self-watch produces a doctrinally precise person whose life contradicts the doctrine. Both must be attended to simultaneously, persistently. 'For by so doing you will save both yourself and your hearers' — the stakes could not be higher: faithful ministry is life or death, for the minister and for those who listen to him.

5.title: Honour and Order in the Family of God
5.overview:
Chapter 5 is one of the most practically detailed sections of any Pauline letter — a series of instructions about specific categories of people within the congregation: older and younger men and women (vv. 1–2), widows of various kinds (vv. 3–16), and elders (vv. 17–25). The chapter's governing principle is the family metaphor: the church is a household, and its members are to relate to one another as members of a family, with the honesty, dignity, and mutual care that family relationships require.

The extended instruction on widows (vv. 3–16) is the longest treatment of a specific social situation in the Pastoral Epistles and reflects the real demographic complexity of the early church. The church had apparently established an official 'order' of widows who were supported by the community and who in return gave themselves to prayer and ministry. Paul's instruction refines this: not all widows qualify for the list; younger widows should remarry and manage households; the burden of supporting widows should fall first on their families, not on the church. These are not harsh distinctions but wise stewardship — protecting the community's resources for those who genuinely have no other provision.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The brief opening instruction sets the tone for the entire chapter: the church is a family, and its members are to be treated as such. An older man is to be addressed as a father; younger men as brothers; older women as mothers; younger women as sisters. The family language is not merely metaphorical; it describes the actual quality of relationship that the gospel creates. People who share the same Father, who are born of the same Spirit, who are members of the same body — they are, in a real sense, family. And family members don't rebuke one another with contempt; they appeal, encourage, and correct with the combination of respect and intimacy that family relationships allow.
verseByVerse.theology: The instruction not to 'rebuke an older man but encourage him as you would a father' reflects the biblical theology of honour that runs from the fifth commandment through the whole of the New Testament. The church does not abolish social distinctions (older/younger, male/female) but reframes them: the older man is honoured not as a social superior but as a father in the family of God. The minister who has learned to address the whole congregation as family — with the genuine warmth and respect that good family relationships involve — has mastered one of the most important skills in pastoral ministry.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Timothy was young, and some of the older men in Ephesus may have resented being corrected by someone younger. Paul's instruction channels that dynamic into the family metaphor: Timothy is not a superior correcting inferiors; he is a younger brother appealing to older brothers and fathers in love.

Now: The pastor who leads with positional authority alone — demanding compliance because he holds the office — has missed Paul's model. The pastor who leads as a member of the family, with the genuine affection and mutual respect that family relationships entail, wins the hearing that authority alone cannot command.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not rebuke an older man but encourage him as you would a father, younger men as brothers, older women as mothers, younger women as sisters, in all purity.
verseByVerse.commentary: The four relationships — father, brother, mother, sister — cover the entire intergenerational range of the congregation. Each relationship carries a specific quality: the father is honoured and gently appealed to; brothers are engaged with the frank equality of peers; mothers are treated with the deep respect of a son who knows his debt; sisters are related to with protective purity. 'In all purity' at the end most immediately qualifies the relationship with younger women — the pastoral relationship with women in the congregation requires a careful intentionality about physical, emotional, and relational boundaries. The minister who thinks of the younger women of his congregation as sisters — with the combination of affection and protective respect that implies — is practising the purity Paul requires.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The extended instruction on widows reflects the church's earliest and most consistent ministry: care for women who have no male protector in a world where widowhood meant social and economic vulnerability. The church from its earliest days had maintained a ministry to widows (Acts 6:1–6; James 1:27), and by Paul's day this had apparently developed into a semi-formal order of widows who were supported by the congregation and who in return gave themselves to prayer and ministry (v. 5).

Paul's instruction introduces important distinctions. A 'true widow' (v. 3, 5, 16) is one who is genuinely alone — without family to care for her, and who has set her hope on God rather than on the pleasures of the world. A widow who has family must be supported by that family: 'if a widow has children or grandchildren, let them first learn to show godliness to their own household and to make some return to their parents, for this is pleasing in the sight of God' (v. 4). The church's resources are to be focused on those who genuinely have no one else. And younger widows — who are still at a stage of life where remarriage and family are appropriate — should not be enrolled in the widows' order but should remarry, bear children, and manage households.
verseByVerse.theology: The statement that 'if anyone does not provide for his relatives, and especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever' (v. 8) is one of the most striking in the Pastoral Epistles. It grounds family care in the theological category of faith: to refuse to care for your family is not merely a social failure but a theological one — a practical denial of the God who himself cares for the vulnerable. The Reformed tradition has always maintained that faith is expressed in works, and that the most immediate sphere of those works is the family. The person who claims to trust God but refuses to care for those nearest to them has shown by their actions what their faith is actually worth.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Ephesian church faced a real pressure: too many widows on the list, not enough resources, and family members who were apparently offloading their elderly relatives onto the church rather than caring for them at home. Paul's instruction protects the church's ability to care for genuine need by requiring families to step up first.

Now: The same dynamic plays out in every congregation that takes seriously its calling to care for the vulnerable. The wise church honours genuine widows and vulnerable members; it also calls families to take responsibility for their own rather than depending on the church as a substitute for family obligation. Both are expressions of love.

verseByVerse.quote: Honor widows who are truly widows. But if a widow has children or grandchildren, let them first learn to show godliness to their own household and to make some return to their parents, for this is pleasing in the sight of God. She who is truly a widow, left all alone, has set her hope on God and continues in supplications and prayers night and day... But if anyone does not provide for his relatives, and especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Honour widows who are truly widows' — the honour includes financial support, as the Deuteronomic instruction to honour parents implies material provision (Deut 5:16; cf. Mark 7:9–13). The description of the true widow who 'has set her hope on God and continues in supplications and prayers night and day' is one of the most beautiful portraits of old age in Scripture — the woman reduced to nothing by the world's reckoning, but whose poverty has stripped away every distraction and left her with what matters most: God, and prayer to God. Anna in Luke 2:36–38 is the living embodiment. The stark contrast with the self-indulgent widow (v. 6) — 'who is self-indulgent is dead even while she lives' — makes the point: the outward condition of widowhood is not determinative; the orientation of the heart is what matters.

verseByVerse.quote: Let a widow be enrolled if she is not less than sixty years of age, having been the wife of one husband, and having a reputation for good works: if she has brought up children, has shown hospitality, has washed the feet of the saints, has cared for the afflicted, and has devoted herself to every good work.
verseByVerse.commentary: The qualifications for the widows' order are the qualifications of a lifetime of faithful service: marital faithfulness, hospitality, service to the saints ('washed the feet' — the most menial domestic service), care for the afflicted, devotion to good works. The widow enrolled in the order is not being honoured because she is old or in need; she is being honoured because her long life has demonstrated the character of a servant of God. Sixty years was a genuine threshold of physical vulnerability in the ancient world. And the requirement that she be 'the wife of one husband' mirrors the requirement for overseers — a one-man woman, characterised by the same conjugal integrity as the one-woman man of 3:2.

verseByVerse.quote: So I would have younger widows marry, bear children, manage their households, and give the adversary no occasion for slander. For some have already strayed after Satan.
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's instruction to younger widows to remarry is sometimes misread as a low view of singleness or of women. It is actually a high view of vocation: the calling to manage a household and raise children is a genuine and honourable calling, not a consolation prize for those who can't manage the spiritual life of the widows' order. The danger Paul identifies is that young widows enrolled in the order become idle, given to gossip and unwanted intrusion — their energy and desire for engagement, without the appropriate outlet of household management and family life, finding destructive channels. 'Give the adversary no occasion for slander' — the church's testimony is always at stake. A congregation where young widows are behaving in ways that bring criticism gives opponents grounds for attacking the gospel itself.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The instructions about elders (vv. 17–25) cover three related matters: the honour due to elders who lead well (vv. 17–18), the process for handling accusations against elders (vv. 19–21), and the caution required in ordaining elders (vv. 22–25). Together they describe a community that is serious about both honouring its leaders and protecting itself from leadership failure.

'Double honour' for elders who rule well — 'especially those who labour in preaching and teaching' — includes both respect and financial remuneration. Paul quotes both the law ('you shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain') and the Lord ('the labourer deserves his wages') as warrant for paying those who give themselves to the ministry of the word. The eldership is a genuine vocation, not a voluntary extra, and those who give themselves to it deserve the material support that allows them to do so.

The instruction on handling accusations against elders (vv. 19–21) balances two dangers: the danger of unfounded accusation destroying a faithful leader (require two or three witnesses), and the danger of protecting a sinning leader from correction (those who persist in sin are to be rebuked before all). The combination of protection and accountability is the mark of a community that takes both justice and truth seriously.
verseByVerse.theology: The principle of 'double honour' for elders who rule well — particularly those who labour in preaching and teaching — reflects the Reformed conviction that the ministry of the word is the primary work of the pastor. Preaching is not one activity among many in pastoral ministry; it is the central act, because through it the word of God does its life-giving work in the congregation. The elder who gives himself to this labour deserves material support that allows him to do it fully — not as an entitlement but as the community's recognition that the work of the word is the work from which all other blessing flows.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Ephesian church had elders who needed both protection (from false accusations) and accountability (some were apparently involved in the false teaching, cf. Acts 20:30). Paul's balanced instruction addresses both: protect the innocent, discipline the guilty, do it in the open without partiality.

Now: The church's most painful crises often involve leadership failure — elders or pastors who have sinned and whose sin has been covered rather than addressed. Paul's instruction is unambiguous: 'those who persist in sin, rebuke in the presence of all, so that the rest may stand in fear.' Transparency in addressing leadership sin, however painful, is the community's protection against the culture of concealment that allows further damage.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the elders who rule well be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in preaching and teaching. For the Scripture says, 'You shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain,' and, 'The laborer deserves his wages.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
‘Rule well’ (kalōs proestōtes) — governing effectively, with the combination of wisdom and care that good leadership requires. ‘Double honour’ — the word timē means both respect and payment, both honour and fee. In a congregation that had apparently been neglecting or under-honouring its leaders, Paul establishes the principle: faithful leadership deserves generous recognition.

The double warrant — from the law (Deut 25:4) and from the Lord Jesus (Luke 10:7) — grounds the practice in the deepest possible soil, and the way Paul introduces them is canonically significant. Both citations are introduced by the single formula ‘the Scripture says’ (legei hē graphē). The second — ‘the labourer deserves his wages’ — is a saying of Jesus, found in Luke 10:7 (and Matt 10:10 in similar form). By placing a word of Jesus under the same rubric of ‘Scripture’ as a Mosaic law text, Paul makes one of the earliest and most explicit statements in the New Testament that the Jesus tradition already carries scriptural authority equal to the Old Testament. Luke’s Gospel, or at least the dominical tradition behind it, was apparently in circulation and recognized as authoritative when Paul wrote in the mid-60s AD — a remarkable canonical data point that anticipates the church’s formal recognition of the Gospels as Scripture in the following century. God’s care for working animals and the Lord’s provision for his missionaries both point to the same principle: those who labour for the community deserve the community’s support.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not admit a charge against an elder except on the evidence of two or three witnesses. As for those who persist in sin, rebuke them in the presence of all, so that the rest may stand in fear. In the presence of God and of Christ Jesus and of the elect angels I charge you to keep these rules without prejudging, doing nothing from partiality.
verseByVerse.commentary: The two-or-three witness requirement (from Deut 19:15) protects leaders from the casual accusation of a disgruntled member. But the requirement to rebuke persistent sinners publicly prevents leaders from hiding behind their office. The solemn charge — 'in the presence of God and of Christ Jesus and of the elect angels' — invokes the heavenly court as witness to Timothy's handling of these matters. Partiality in either direction — protecting a friend, or joining the mob against someone unpopular — is a form of injustice in the sight of the One who judges without partiality. Church discipline is always conducted before an audience of One, and that One sees everything.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be hasty in the laying on of hands, nor take part in the sins of others; keep yourself pure... The sins of some people are conspicuous, going before them to judgment, but the sins of others appear later. So also good works are conspicuous, and even those that are not cannot remain hidden.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Do not be hasty in the laying on of hands' — ordination, once given, is difficult to reverse, and a hasty ordination of an unproven person makes the ordaining congregation complicit in whatever damage follows. Paul's point is not suspicion of candidates but realism about human character: some sins are visible before ordination and make the problem obvious; others only emerge later, after the person has been entrusted with leadership. The same applies to good works: some are immediately visible; others are hidden and emerge over time. The lesson: be patient, observe carefully, and ordain slowly. What is truly in a person will eventually become visible — for good or ill. Give it time.

Then, mid-list, an oddly personal aside: "no longer drink only water, but use a little wine for the sake of your stomach." Timothy — perhaps over-correcting against a culture of excess, or wary of the false teachers' food rules (4:3) — was drinking only water, often unsafe in ancient cities, and his health was paying for it. Paul's counsel is medicinal and humane: God is not honoured by a ruined stomach, and bodily care is not unspiritual. A small verse that guards a large truth: asceticism is not holiness.

6.title: Godliness with Contentment Is Great Gain
6.overview:
The final chapter of 1 Timothy circles back to the twin concerns of the whole letter — false teaching and disordered living — and resolves them in the great climactic passage on the fight of faith (vv. 11–16) and the charge to guard the deposit (vv. 20–21). Between these bookends, Paul addresses slaves and masters (vv. 1–2), the false teachers' love of money (vv. 3–10), Timothy's personal charge as a man of God (vv. 11–16), and instructions for the wealthy (vv. 17–19).

The centrepiece of the chapter — and perhaps of the whole letter — is vv. 6–10 and their theological inversion of the false teachers' motto: they had apparently taught that 'godliness is a means of gain' (v. 5). Paul turns this inside out: 'godliness with contentment is great gain' (v. 6). The gain is not financial; it is the deep, settled sufficiency of a person who has found in God what the world cannot provide and therefore needs nothing more than food and clothing and the God who gives both.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul's instruction to slaves and masters is brief but theologically grounded. Slaves are to 'regard their own masters as worthy of all honour, so that the name of God and the teaching may not be reviled' (v. 1). The motive is evangelical: the behaviour of Christian slaves in a pagan household is a testimony, positive or negative, to the God they serve. A slave who behaves with dignity and diligence commends the gospel; a slave who uses the freedom of the gospel as an excuse for contempt of masters brings the gospel into disrepute. The instruction to Christian slaves with Christian masters — not to treat them with less respect because they are 'brothers' — addresses the opposite danger: familiarity breeding contempt within the Christian community.
verseByVerse.theology: Paul does not here call for the abolition of slavery — the social revolution will come by the logic of the gospel working through history, not by immediate political action — but he seeds the ground for it by calling Christian masters and slaves 'brothers.' The equality of standing before God inevitably generates pressure on social institutions that deny that equality. It is the leaven of Philemon writ large. The Reformed tradition has understood this as the gospel's indirect but powerful social influence: the proclamation of human dignity before God eventually reshapes the institutions that deny it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Roman economy was built on slave labour. For a Christian slave to be insolent or negligent — even on the grounds that Christ had made them free — would have made the gospel deeply unattractive to the slaveholding class that needed to hear it. Paul's instruction is missiologically wise: commend the gospel by the quality of your work.

Now: The principle translates into every employment relationship: the Christian employee who works 'as for the Lord' (Col 3:23), with diligence and integrity, commends the faith more powerfully than a thousand arguments. The 'name of God and the teaching' are always at stake in how Christians behave in ordinary social relationships.

verseByVerse.quote: Let all who are under a yoke as bondservants regard their own masters as worthy of all honor, so that the name of God and the teaching may not be reviled. Those who have believing masters must not be disrespectful on the ground that they are brothers; rather they must serve all the better since those who benefit by their good service are believers and beloved.
verseByVerse.commentary: The 'name of God and the teaching' are the dual stakes: God's reputation and the gospel's credibility. Both are embodied in the behaviour of God's people in the world. The instruction to Christian slaves with Christian masters is particularly nuanced: the temptation to use the brotherhood as an excuse for laxity is real — if my master is my brother, surely he will overlook my failures? Paul says the opposite: serve all the better. The person who benefits from your work is a beloved fellow-believer; serve them as you would want to be served. The gospel creates better employees and better employers, not a levelling that abolishes the distinction of function.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul returns to the false teachers with his most pointed description yet. Those who 'teach a different doctrine' and do not agree with 'the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and the teaching that accords with godliness' are 'puffed up with conceit and understand nothing' (v. 4). The pathology of false teaching — conceited ignorance — is matched by its fruit: 'an unhealthy craving for controversy and for quarrels about words, which produce envy, dissension, slander, evil suspicions, and constant friction' (vv. 4–5). False doctrine is not merely wrong; it is destructive, generating in the community the very things that the gospel is designed to overcome.

The false teachers had apparently used religion as a commercial opportunity — treating godliness as a means of financial gain. Paul's counter is the great inversion: 'godliness with contentment is great gain' (v. 6). But the gain is not material. The person who has food and clothing and God has everything. And the person who pursues wealth as the goal of life — whether through religion or other means — has 'wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many pangs' (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: The famous statement 'the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil' (v. 10) is often misquoted as 'money is the root of all evil.' Paul is more precise on both counts. It is the love of money (philargyria — the craving, the disordered devotion to wealth) that is the root — not money itself, which is morally neutral and can be used for great good (cf. vv. 17–19). And it is 'a root of all kinds of evil' — not the only root, but a root that produces a surprising variety of evils when it takes hold. Reformed theology identifies the love of money as a form of idolatry: it sets wealth in the place of God, expecting from it the security, the significance, and the satisfaction that only God can provide. The result is always disappointment and destruction.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The false teachers in Ephesus had apparently monetised their ministry — teaching for profit, using godliness as a commercial strategy. Paul's devastating critique is that they had discovered how to make religion pay while knowing nothing of what religion actually is.

Now: The prosperity gospel is the most visible contemporary version of this — 'godliness as a means of gain,' with wealth and health presented as evidence of faith. Paul's answer is the same: the gospel does not promise prosperity but contentment; not wealth but sufficiency; not the abundance of things but the presence of God who is himself the great gain.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone teaches a different doctrine and does not agree with the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and the teaching that accords with godliness, he is puffed up with conceit and understands nothing. He has an unhealthy craving for controversy and for quarrels about words, which produce envy, dissension, slander, evil suspicions, and constant friction among people who are depraved in mind and deprived of the truth, imagining that godliness is a means of gain.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Sound words' (hygiainousai logoi) — the medical metaphor runs through the Pastorals: some words are healthy and life-giving; others are diseased and infectious. The false teacher's pathology is spiritual pride ('puffed up with conceit') combined with intellectual emptiness ('understands nothing'). It is a particularly dangerous combination: confident ignorance, dressed up as spiritual authority, generating controversy that destroys community. The five-fold list of the controversy's fruits — envy, dissension, slander, evil suspicions, constant friction — is a clinical description of what false teaching does to a congregation. These are not incidental side effects; they are the inevitable harvest of words that do not accord with the teaching that produces godliness.

verseByVerse.quote: But godliness with contentment is great gain, for we brought nothing into the world, and we cannot take anything out of the world. But if we have food and clothing, with these we will be content. But those who desire to be rich fall into temptation, into a snare, into many senseless and harmful desires that plunge people into ruin and destruction. For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils. It is through this craving that some have wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many pangs.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Godliness with contentment' — the Greek word for contentment is autarkeia, the Stoic term for self-sufficiency. Paul adopts the word and fills it with new content: Christian contentment is not Stoic self-sufficiency (the inner fortress of the self against the world) but God-sufficiency — the settled conviction that in God I have what I need, and that what I have is enough. 'We brought nothing into the world, and we cannot take anything out' — one of the great levelling observations of Scripture, echoing Job 1:21 and Ecclesiastes. The bare fact of our poverty at birth and death frames the whole of our earthly accumulation as borrowed, temporary, and ultimately inconsequential. Food and clothing — the minimum of physical sustenance — are enough if they come with the great gain of godliness. The love of money, by contrast, is not a stable desire but a compulsive one: it cannot be satisfied by obtaining money, because the obtaining always reveals more to want. Its victims are 'pierced' — a vivid image of the self-inflicted wounds of covetousness.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The climax of the letter is a direct, personal charge to Timothy — one of the most stirring passages in all of Paul's writing. 'But as for you, O man of God, flee these things. Pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, steadfastness, gentleness. Fight the good fight of the faith. Take hold of eternal life to which you were called' (vv. 11–12). The contrast with the false teachers is total: they pursue wealth and controversy; Timothy is to pursue righteousness and godliness; they grasp at earthly gain; Timothy is to take hold of eternal life.

The charge is grounded in Timothy's own confession — made 'in the presence of many witnesses' (v. 12), probably at his baptism or ordination — and in the parallel confession of Jesus Christ, who 'in his testimony before Pontius Pilate made the good confession' (v. 13). Timothy's faithfulness is not solitary; it participates in the same pattern of confessing witness that the Lord himself established before the Roman governor. And the final doxology (vv. 15–16) is the most overwhelming in the Pastoral Epistles — the 'blessed and only Sovereign, the King of kings and Lord of lords, who alone has immortality, who dwells in unapproachable light.' This is the One in whose name and before whose face Timothy is to keep the commandment, until the appearing of the Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.theology: The title 'King of kings and Lord of lords' (v. 15) applied to God the Father — and later applied to the Lord Jesus in Revelation 17:14 and 19:16 — is the ultimate statement of divine supremacy against all rival claims to ultimate authority: Caesar, the gods of Ephesus, the powers of the age. The God who dwells in unapproachable light — whom no human has seen or can see (v. 16) — is infinitely beyond every human attempt to domesticate or manage the divine. The Reformed tradition has always insisted on divine transcendence as the foundation of divine sovereignty: God is not one power among many, adjustable to human convenience, but the blessed and only Sovereign before whom every knee will bow and every tongue confess.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Timothy's confession 'before many witnesses' had been made in a specific historical moment — at his ordination or baptism, in front of the congregation. That public commitment is now Paul's appeal: remember what you said; live consistently with it; don't let the hardness of the task or the pressure of the false teachers cause you to retreat from the confession you made in public.

Now: Every Christian has made a public confession — in baptism, in confirmation, in church membership vows. Paul's charge to Timothy is the charge that every confession implies: keep the commandment; fight the good fight; take hold of what you confessed. The confession is not merely a past moment but a present and future commitment.

verseByVerse.quote: But as for you, O man of God, flee these things. Pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, steadfastness, gentleness. Fight the good fight of the faith. Take hold of eternal life to which you were called and about which you made the good confession in the presence of many witnesses.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Man of God' — a title used in the Old Testament for Moses (Deut 33:1), Samuel (1 Sam 9:6), Elijah (1 Kings 17:18), and Elisha (2 Kings 4:7). Timothy is placed in the tradition of those who stood for the word of God against the compromises of their age. 'Flee these things' — the love of money, the false teaching, the controversies. There are things a Christian must flee, not fight. Then 'pursue' — six things in a list that covers the whole person: righteousness (right standing and right living), godliness (whole-life orientation toward God), faith and love (the twin pillars of Christian life), steadfastness (the patient endurance of what cannot be changed), gentleness (the controlled strength of the meek). Then 'fight' — the athletic contest of faith, sustained until the end. Then 'take hold' — the active, deliberate grasping of eternal life, which is simultaneously a gift (you were called) and a commitment (you made the good confession).

verseByVerse.quote: I charge you in the presence of God, who gives life to all things, and of Christ Jesus, who in his testimony before Pontius Pilate made the good confession, to keep the commandment unstained and free from reproach until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ, which he will display at the proper time—he who is the blessed and only Sovereign, the King of kings and Lord of lords, who alone has immortality, who dwells in unapproachable light, whom no one has ever seen or can see. To him be honor and eternal dominion. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary: The charge is issued in the presence of God who gives life and Christ Jesus who bore witness — and that double divine presence makes it as solemn as anything Paul writes. 'Keep the commandment unstained and free from reproach until the appearing' — the whole of Timothy's ministry is a holding action, a faithful keeping until Jesus comes. And then the doxology: six attributes of the living God, stacked like a crescendo — 'blessed and only Sovereign' (supreme happiness and absolute uniqueness), 'King of kings and Lord of lords' (all authority subject to him), 'alone has immortality' (he is the source of all life; creatures only have life lent to them), 'dwells in unapproachable light' (his holiness is not merely intense but categorically different from everything created), 'whom no one has ever seen or can see' (the infinite beyond-ness of God). To this One — honour and eternal dominion. The proper response to such a God is not cool assent but overwhelming doxology: Amen.

verseByVerse.ref: 6:17–21 – Instructions to the Rich / Guard the Deposit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The letter closes with two final movements: a pastoral instruction for wealthy members of the congregation (vv. 17–19) and a solemn final charge to Timothy to guard the deposit entrusted to him (vv. 20–21). Together they form a fitting conclusion to a letter that has been concerned throughout with the right use of resources — whether theological (the gospel) or material (money).

The instruction to the rich is carefully nuanced: Paul does not condemn wealth but the wrong relationship to wealth — haughtiness, uncertainty of hope, the setting of hope on riches rather than on God. The positive alternative is not poverty but generosity: 'be generous and ready to share' (v. 18). The generous person is 'storing up treasure for themselves as a good foundation for the future' — the kingdom investment principle that Jesus had taught and that Paul here applies to the wealthy in the Ephesian congregation. Wealth rightly used is not an obstacle to the kingdom but an instrument of it.
verseByVerse.theology: The phrase 'guard the deposit entrusted to you' (tēn parathēkēn phylaxon, v. 20) is the distillation of everything Paul has been saying about sound doctrine, faithful ministry, and the church as the pillar and buttress of the truth. The 'deposit' is the gospel — the trustworthy sayings, the mystery of godliness, the sound words of the Lord Jesus Christ. It has been given to Timothy as a steward; his task is to keep it intact, to hand it on without diminishment or distortion, to protect it against the 'irreverent babble and contradictions of what is falsely called knowledge.' The Reformation used exactly this language — 'the faith once for all delivered to the saints' (Jude 3) — as the warrant for recovering the gospel that had been buried under centuries of tradition. Every faithful minister is a guardian of this deposit.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The wealthy members of the Ephesian church — in a city where the economy was partly driven by the temple trade and where commercial success was associated with the favour of Artemis — needed to understand that their wealth was not a sign of divine approval but a trust to be administered for the sake of others.

Now: The church in wealthy societies faces the same challenge: what does it mean to be 'rich in good works, generous, ready to share'? The answer is not a fixed percentage or a tax calculation but a whole-life orientation toward generosity — the kind of openhanded, joyful, gospel-motivated giving that stores up treasure in the only account that will survive the death of the world's economy.

verseByVerse.quote: As for the rich in this present age, charge them not to be haughty, nor to set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches, but on God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy. They are to do good, to be rich in good works, to be generous and ready to share, thus storing up treasure for themselves as a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of that which is truly life.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The uncertainty of riches' is a phrase that deserves meditation: riches are, by nature, uncertain. They come and go; they are vulnerable to inflation, theft, market collapse, illness, death. To set your hope on something uncertain is to build on sand. But God 'richly provides us with everything to enjoy' — the creation-theology of chapter 4 reappears: the material world is God's gift for enjoyment, not something to be despised or hoarded. The generous person who uses wealth for good works is not giving away enjoyment; they are discovering it — the deep joy of being a conduit of God's generosity rather than a reservoir that only accumulates. 'That which is truly life' — eternal life, real life, the life that riches can neither buy nor replace.

verseByVerse.quote: O Timothy, guard the deposit entrusted to you. Avoid the irreverent babble and contradictions of what is falsely called 'knowledge,' for by professing it some have swerved from the faith. Grace be with you.
verseByVerse.commentary: The final charge is the letter's summation. 'O Timothy' — the personal vocative, the apostle's hand on the young man's shoulder. 'Guard the deposit' — the gospel, the sound words, the trustworthy sayings, the mystery of godliness. It is not his to innovate; it is his to guard and transmit. 'Falsely called knowledge' (gnōsis) — the proto-Gnostic system that claimed access to hidden spiritual truth — is the lie against which the deposit must be guarded. Some have 'swerved' (the archer's miss of 1:6 reappears) by professing it. The final word is not law but grace: 'Grace be with you.' The letter that began with grace — 'grace, mercy, and peace' to Timothy (1:2) — ends with grace: the unearned, overflowing, sustaining grace of the Lord Jesus Christ. Everything in between — the doctrine, the discipline, the doxology — is the shape that grace takes in the household of God.
